CYCLING AND CYCLISTS.
No. V.—CYCLING ACCIDENTS, AND HOW TO AVOID THEDL
Br T. S. JOHNSTON (CONTRIBUTOR TO THZ "LUSH CYCLIST, " &c.).

If one were to judge from the number of cycling accidents reported almost daily in the press, one would probably come to the conclusion that the name "safety," so generally applied to the modern bicycle, is a misnomer. For, even in the days of what old-timers love to call "the good old ordinary," accidents were neither so frequent nor so serious u they are to-day. It cannot, however, be said with truth that this state of affairs is wholly due to any Specific virtues possessed by the bicycle of other days, but rather to the many changes which have taken place in the world of wheels since the advent of the pneumatic-tyred safety. Although at first sight

div.head: CROPPER FROM THE GIDDY HEIGHT
div.p: A CROPPER FROM THE GIDDY HEIGHT

of a 56in. ordinary may appear more dangerous than a spill from the low•built type of to-day, those who have been through both experiences will agree that the latter is the least preferable of the two. The dropped handle-bar of the modern mount generally ensures the rider ping straight to earth on his head or shoulder when he croppers, which accounts for the frequency with which breakage of the coilar-bone and contusions of the skull figure among the casualties of to-day. In falling from the high bicycle the rider frequently tumbled a complete somersault, and escaped with a severe shaking and a few body bruises, or if he took a more direct course to Mother Earth his chances of saving himself were greater than those of a rider hurled from the modern type. This may, to some extent, explain the increase in the number of serious and fatal cycling accidents, but it must further be remembered that in the days of the high bicycle, cyclists were a small brother- hood of lusty, muscular young fellows, whereas to-day the vast army of cyclists is recruited from all sorts and conditions of men and women.
That a great number of the at cidents which befall cyclists might be

PREVENTED BY A LITTLE FORITHOrGHT on the part of the riders themselves is an undoubted fact, and it is with the purpose of pointing out where trouble begins and how it may be avoided that this article is written. A very common error with new riders, and one that is responsible for no small proportion of the accidents that occur, is neglect of the machine itself! The modern bicycle is a very delicate piece of workmanship, and should not be treated as if it were a wheelbarrow. When it comes from the maker's, the first thing the purchaser should do is to go thoroughly over it, examining all the nuts and brake fittings with special care. Every nut and bolt should be tested to see that they are properly tightened,and the wheels and pedals should be spun mind to see if they are correctly adjusted. The chain should also be carefully examined to make certain that the bolt and nut holding it together are secure. This latter is a most important precaution. "The rider should also see that the saddle and handle- bar are firmly fastened, for the sudden loosening of one of these may cause a fatal ending to a ride. These precautions should be repeated before every ride, for it will be found that neglect of them is a most prolific source of accidents.

The brake, it is scarcely necessary to remark, is a vital part of one's machine. It is the cyclist's life saving apparatus, and should therefore receive the most punctilious attention. A brake that will not act promptly and efficiently in a moment of danger is

div.head: WORSE THAN NO BRAKE AT ALL,
div.p: WORSE THAN NO BRAKE AT ALL,

for, in the former case, the cyclist i; likely to become flurried, and both literally and meta- phorically upset, when he finds his machine getting out of control, and his brake absolutely useless. Tinder these circumstances, he has a choice of three courses. If the descent to the foot of a hill be clear, and devoid of traffic, he had better keep a firm seat, and let his machine go. But if he cannot see the bottom of the hill, and there be an adjacent hedge, he had better steer straight for that, when he will probably escape with a few scratches. If, however,xuone of these courses are open to him, he may appls- a very effective brake by lifting one foot off the pedal, and inserting it between the fork crown and the tyre. This should be done very cautiously and slowly, as a too sudden application of pressure may mean a broken leg. If the machine be fitted with mudguards this cannot be done, but the foot may then be applied very carefully to the side of the tyre, in front of the forks. It takes a little nerve for a novice to perform this feat successfully, and excitable riders should not attempt it unless as a last resource. Many riders of long experience use no other brake save this, and back pedalling, but it is a wise rider who carries a brake under all circumstances.

div.head: 8/DE-SLIP IS A BUGBEAR
div.p: 8/DE-SLIP IS A BUGBEAR

to the modern cyclist, and is one of the few disadvan- tages that the pneumatic tyre brought in its train. Very few cyclists have not at some time or other experienced the terrors of the side-slip, when the bicycle suddenly goes cavorting off at its own free will, while the rider makes frantic and generally futile efforts to keep it upright. This is one of the moat dangerous of the cyclist's enemies. It lurks in greasy tram lines, and other unexpected spots, and many are the broken limbs for which it has been responsible. Various devices have been introduced to abate this nuisance, but it is still flourishing. The best way to avoid side-slip is to cultivate an even and graceful style of pedalling, for it is the clumsy, erratic pedaller who is its greatest victim. It is also advisable to pump the tyres a little harder than usual on those days when the roads are just moist enough to favour the side- slip, and greasy tram-lines can be Safely negotiated U, they are crossed at an angle of 45 degrees. `The writer does not, under any circumstances, recommend the use cf toe-clips, but on those days when the side-slip is abroad in the land the practice is more than usually dangerous. Some time ago young man had his leg fractured in three places under such circumstances, as he was unable to ex- tricate his foot while falling. Verb. sap.

Neglect of what is known as the rule of the road Is another frequent cause of accidents. Especially •ts this fault to be found among what may be called the "new" cyclists, who have taken up the pastime anise Fashion smiled favourably on the wheel. Many of these riders scatter themselves indiscrimi- nately across the highway, and frequently they are to be found indulging in gymkhana tricks, to the danger of other wheeltnen. Riders who neglect to conform to the recognised rules of the road are deserving of no sympathy in case of accident, and are, not likely to find any in a court of justice. A cyclist should ALWAYS KEEP TO THE LEFT-HAND mon of the road, except when passing a vehicle going in the same direction, which should be passed on the night-hand side, the rider ringing his bell as he Approaches the vehicle to be passed. The same rule ~„-applies if the rider wishes to pass another cyclist •who is travelling in the same direction. The sing- -s.ing of a bicycle bell is in itself something of an _art, and should be done with discretion. Cyclists who wish to give pedestrians or other riders warn- ing of their approach should sound their bells when :About twenty yards away, and again when a little -nearer. This will give the person warned time to collect his thoughts and decide how taact, whereas, if the rider does not give notice of approach until _quite close to the paten to be passel, it is just !Possible that a wholesale mix-up may take place rthtough some sudden evolution of the latter. Very often, the cyclist will find it advisable not to sound his bell at all when approaching a pedestrian, but simply to steer round him. A nervous pedestrian -can accomplish wonders if a cyclist's bell suddenly , peal out Cu his ears.

CYCLINCi IN CITIES is, of course, always more dangerous than country .riding, 13-at even here a little more care considerably •niinimises the risks. The cyclist who has much city cycling to do will find it a most advisable -rtiiiins, to ride with a low saddle, which plan will

div.head: PATBIST SELF-RAISING FLOU It
div.p: PATBIST SELF-RAISING FLOU It
ly and easily to put either foot to
himself in a tight place. fle

should also lean to dismount equally smartly from both sides of hi machine, and to dismount by the pedal, which is he best and most expeditious method of getting of. ''.--t.ernerS should be turned with the utmost caution, sad the bell should always be loudly sounded first. Tie rider should not keep too close to the kerbstone, for these is always the possibility of some Person stepping off the footpath suddenly, and bringing him over. To be able to ride very slowly is a necescary accomplishment for the city cyclist, for there are times when, in a congested thoroughfare, it is necessary to move at a pace at which it is pretty difficalt to retain the balance of the machine. The writer has found "keep moving' to be a good motto when cycling in thick traffic, but if the rider loses his nerve in a crowd, and feels that he must dismount, he should always signal to the driver of the vehicle behind ere he attempts to jump off. Numerous accidents have occurred through neglect of this simple precaution. Indecision is another frequent cause of accidents to city cyclists. Everyone kncws the difficulty captains of large steamers often experience through the panic- stricken movements of people in small boats who are afraid of being run down. Drivers of vehicles are often placed in the same position through the 71gr5g evolutions of some nerve-paralysed cyclist. The cyclist who rides nuch in the city should be quick to decide and act when a difficulty presents itself, for nothing is more conducive to accidents than nervous timidity. Riding with long lace' in one's shoes is A VERY DAIGHROUS HABIT, and should be rigidly g-uarded against; for the laces are liable to catch in tbs chain, and cause a serious fall. Ladies are common defaulters in this respect. There are, of course, innumerable possibilities of accident ii cycling, but in the above will be found almost all those that can be escaped by the exercise of ordinary vigilance and forethought. Such accidents as are caused by the breakdown of faulty machines are common, and the only way to guard against these is to steer clear of the "cheap and nasty" type of bicycle altogether, purchasing only a machine of recognised merit. Accidents caused by animals are of that class which no amount of fore- thought can guard against, and these are un- doubtedly too common to be agreeable. Dogs are the chief source of trouble, and there are few riders of any experience who cannot recall to mind some unpleasant experience in which the canine friend of man played a prominent part. But after all is said and done it would be a poor sort of pastime into which some possibility of accident or mishap did not enter. Comparing the risks of cycling with those of the hunting field, the balance is largely in favour of the former, and it must be added to the credit of the cycle that people do not treat it with the same amount of respect as they do the home. Very few ladies or gentlemen will go direct from the equestrian school to the hunting field, but thousands think nothing of trusting their lives anywhere in the streets of large cities on the strength of an experience gained in the quietude of a cycling school. Could the force of folly further go?

div.head: REF USED.
div.p: REF USED.

A return was issued on Saturday MI the licences re- fused in 1897 by the Justices of the Pelee in each linens sing district in England and Waite. showing the ground of refusal and the result of any appeal made. Its Lan- cashire there was in the Amounderness district one re- fusal on the ground that the licence was not reqnired. In the Bolton district the same reason was assigncd, to- gether with a statement that the premises had been un- occupied for some time. In the North Longsdals district, in the Ornsskirk district, and in the St. Helens district licenees were refused on the grounds of differ- derlyness and for other seasons. In the St. Helens case alone was an appeal made, but here the allegation was that not only was the house disorderly, but it was frf (planted by bad characters. The appeal was dismissed With costs. The borough returns show that in Man- chester there were ten refusals of victuallers' licences and twenty-four ef beerhouse licences, while five " other " licences were also refused. In the victuallers' licences return one licence was refused for misconduct, and nine of the house,. were pulled down or closed. Of the beerhouse licences eight were refused fcr miscon- duct, 15 houses were pulled down or closed, and one licence was given up—" not rEquired." Of the " other" licences all the houses were closed. Altogether there were in Manchester seven appeals, of which three were successful. In Salford there were but three re- fusals the grounds being in the first case that the house was disorderly, in the second that the applicant failed to produce satisfactory evidence of good character, and in the third that the house was not used for the put. poses for which it was intended. The total number of licences refused in England and Wales was 196, of which 94 were victuallers' licences, 70 beerhouse licences, and 32 " other " Teere were 73 a ppea!a to quarter sessions, of which 32 were successful.

MY Does Mimi, A very attractive hat in turquoise-blue straw is trimmed round the crown with soft folds of white chiffon, on the edge of which were appliques of fine black Chantilly lace. In front is a true- lover's knot, formed of narrow black ribbon velvet, wired to stand out well from the chiffon, and caught in the centre with a steel buckle. The brim of the hat is straight in front, but it curves over in the mushroom shape at the back, and inside, nestling on the hair, are clusters of pinkiroses.

A fashionalL3 toque is of fancy Tuscan straw in a natural shade, trimmed with white silk gauze, draped over yellow ganz,, and caught at the left side with a paste buck:e, set in oxydised silver. On the left side are some double cstrich feathers, those underneath being yellow, and those altove white, which gives a shot elftct, and makes the feathers tone with the double draperies of silk gauze.

A charming bonret has a ruche of fancy satin straw at the clip of the fashionable Parma violet shade, and a draped crown of black gauze, striped with gold tinsel threads. In front are knots ef chiffon to match the brim, caught with paste buckles, and a spray cf lilies•of-the-valley and foliage stand up at the ,ide.

A very novel mock], known as the pinafore coat, is very useful for wear over blouses where a light, smart, eact is desired, while preserving the coat shape at the waist. This is quite Parisian in origin, and is really useful either with a blouse or sleeveless vest, the top showing and forming a yoke above the coat. The fronts hang loose at the extreme edge, but can be secured under the revers to give a closer effect. A gown suitable for wear at the seaside, gar. den parties or boating, could be made of dark blue linen, with blue and white drill for vest and sleeves. A gown would look most effective in blue serge, with blue or white foulard or drill. A muslin skirt and separate blouse should be entirely distinct from the foundation, as whether cleaned or washed, it is quite unnecessary to have the slip cleaned as well, and the trouble of unpicking at the waist is obviated. The slip, if of average quality silk, will not required to be lined, but should have a narrow facing of linen or muslin at the edge, this completely covered by the balayeuse of ailk which goes inside the skirt.

A costume suitable either for tesinis or boating, is of white drill, trimmed with white cotton braid and very narrow pleated frills of the drill. Many of the foulards prepared for summer wear are accompanied by fichus, and it is quite the fashion to trim the bodice in fichu fashion with innumer• able frills of soft material. Necessarily, these frills are duplicated on the skirt, and the whole gown becomes of the most elaborate description. The new flounced skirts are now generally worn, and those copied from Parisian models are graceful and becoming, but the average dressmaker is not successful in getting the requisite trail or the graceful folds, and invariably puts too much fulness in front. Bluet shades are almost as fashionable for even- ing gowns as for day wear, and vivid turquoise trimmings are fashionable on black gowns, com- bined with bright electric-blue sequins, which are extremely light in colour under the now general electric-light, and these seem to have superseded the duller turquoise jewels. Amber, tangerine, and yellow are most fashionable relief tints, and are even worn with blue, but are really lovely on black or white, more especially for evening wear. A lovely gown is of soft pink pectu de note, with trimmings of black la6be velvet ribbon, and the trained skirt embroidered with little stars in sequins and jet cabochons, and set off by rosettes of the velvet behiS ribbon. The bodice is entirely of the embroidered silk, the low bodice outlined with a superb passementerie in jet and coral. Banded bodices are general on evening gowns, and jewelled buckles are a feature on these bands. Your lovinst JENNIE

div.head: rnE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JULY 1, 1898.
div.p: rnE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JULY 1, 1898.
"WOMEN'S CHAT."

The recent operatic performance in the Waterloo Chamber at Windsor castle, was the first that had taken place there since the death of Prince Henry of Batten- berg, who with Princess Henry was the life and soul of such entertainments.TheQueen has long expressed a wish to hear the two f amous singers M. Jean and M. Edouard de Reszke, and it was really this desire that led to the command for a performance of "Rome, et Juliette," at ' Windsor. At the last moment however M. Jean de Reszke was prevented through indisposition from sine- log the part of Romeo, which was undertaken by M. Salem rbe performance was arranged to take place heft re the return of Princess Henry of Battenberg from Germany. to whom it could only have been frought , with painful memories. Several members of our Royal Family take consider- I able interest in the drama, many of them delighting to take part in theatrical performances. But so far none have emulated the example of Queen Mary, who, en- couraged by her father King Henry the VIII, frequently appeared before the Court, when a girl, as the principae dancer in ballets and pantomimes. By the way, the dithyrambics,or songs in honour of Bacchus,which gave birth to dramatic representations, are as ancient as the worship of Bacchus, and there is little doubt but that the ceremonies of his mysteries gave rise to the pomp and illusions of the theatre. Many of the splendid ex- hibitions upon the stage for the entertainment of the people of Athens and Rome, were performed upon the festivals of Bacchue, and gave occasion to all those who were employed in them, whether for singing, dancing, or reciting, servants fa Bacchus. At Athens, the re- mains of the temple ef Bacchus which was the first theatre in the world, may be seen For the celebration of the approaching accession of their young Queen, the Dutch are making the most elaborate preparations. The procession will consist of some 12,000 persons, and places along the route are already being offered, and paid for. The Coronation Medal of Queen Wilhelmina, who, on the evening of the 31st day of August will assume the reins of govern- ment is of silver, and about three inches in diameter. It bears a bust of the Queen, with the legend " Wilhel- mina Konine,en der Nederlanden " round the circumfer- ence, and the inscription" The crown of a Queen is the love of her people "in Dutch, across the diameter. On the reverse side is a figure is Peace, with the Royal Palace of Amsterdam in the backgrrund. The young Queen is an ardent philatilist, and she has a rare collec- tion of Dutch stamps. Her youthfal Majesty is also very enthusiastic on horticulture,and knows her botany well. Her favourite flower is the tulip. The children of Holland arc early. trained in the habits of industry. Quite tiny folks assist with the butter and cheese making, and girls who have not yet left childhood behind them, carry on their heads heavy baskets of fish, and green things from the garden,schich thy all in the streets. The small white muslin cap which, in most localities, covers the heads of the little girls, transforms the rosiest face into one of maturity. The hair beneath this is parted in the middle, and plastered cl,ase to the sides of the brow. Not a curl of childhood, nor a single lain' is allowed to peep beneath the prim little cap. Over every pair of young shoulders is crossed a demure little shawl,and every girl wears an I apron of c arse blue linen over the black frock, made so' long as to cover the white wooden pattens, and black stockings. When not at their work, the fingers of these little girls are nearly always occupied with knittinr woollen hose. I

The Erly Rising Association held Rs annuli rneAkt: on Midsummer Day,at f unriqe ,cm the tap of Parliament Hill,Hampstead. The association has been in existence ten years,and members are not only expected to rise daily with the run,but proclaim upon every possible occasion :he gospel of early rising to their less energetic friends. A larger membership is desired, but the association is scarcely likely to be overwhelmed with applications,un• til_a little more latitude is allowed.

Many of the Royalties ;f Europe have a very praise- worthy,but at the same time surely somewhat inconve- nient habit of getting up early in the day. The Empress nf Austria still continues to rise about half-past three,the Kaiser is generally About by five,while the King of Italy's hour of rising is six, as is that of the King of Sweden, and King Charles of Roumania. The noises of London are receiving much attention at the presf nt time,amone them being—church bells. These it i 3 said, were useful enough in days when there as no other way of letting people know that it was time to go to church, but in these nineteenth century end days, when even an office boy c-in sport a watch, they ate a ridiculous anachronism. There is very little doubt that in crowded cities and towrs,church bells are (-Item an in. tolerable nuisance,but few of us would care to SPO them I utterly extinct. In the stillness of the country they are deliet;ttul, and generally arpreciated, even by those to whom they are most familiar. The origin of the bell is lost; we find it already ib use in the earliest records of human society. Earlier than M'r', Egyptian festivals of the god Osiris began with bril ringing. It is believed, however, that church bells were first used to summon worshippers, by Paulinus, Bishop of Nola, in Campania, (AD. 400.) Still these were but hand bells. Bells in towers are not known to be earlier than the ninth century. About the thirteenth century church bells began to increase in size, and were dedicated to their functions with holy rites, frequently bearing names and till more often pious inscriptions. They were held to drive away evil spirits from the pass- ing soul (the passing hell), to disperse lghtening etc. At the present time, the largest bell in actual use in Western Etvrope, next to our 't Great Pauli is that at Rouen, which weighs :6 tons, lcwt. Where the narrow satin ribbon is not, the sequin is. The idea of the moment is to introduce animals such as serpents, lizards, griffens on tea gowns, evening wraps, or skirts of silk and satin, carried out in sequins, laidl one over another, and irridescent in their coloring. The mode though is scarcely a fascinating one. A few nights back I followed a woman into a theatre who was wearing a white satin cloak, round the neck of which reposed a—sequin—cobra. In the half light the effect was just a little startling. Tail coats are gaining ground and several Paris models possess tails which hang halfway down the skirt.—These tails are usually lined with some contrasting tint, a ruche of the same being placed on the inside of the hem of the skirt. Like the greater number of our modes, this latest is suited only to tall and slender women, and even with them, is often far from being a success. Every woman ought to make herself as presentabl SR possible. Hands whether beautiful or otherwise, ould be well cared for, the nails should be nicely kept and if e sh the hand is very large, and net of a pretty shape, gloves should fit especially well, and when possible be of a dark color. It was a Frenchman who said that a pretty woman with bad teeth was never lovely, and an ugly woman with tood teeth, never plain. Teeth are more remarkable in some people than in others,hut in all cases well cared for teeth add much to the gnod appearance of their possessors. Then, women witb thin necks and long chins, should always wear a Foft frill or ruche, in. of the high stiff collar, which has the effect 91 bringing into greater prominence their bad Points. Again well-arranged hair is always attractive. If it has come out from ill.health or other causes, then a worm° should wear a tourpee. They are so built now-a-days, as to defy detection, and anything is better than offending the aye by patches of baldness. Savoury Omelet Take two eggs, season with pepper and salt, whisk until light, and creamy, and add half a dessert spoonful of finely chopped parsley. Put a knob of butter the size of a walnut into a small omelet-pan and let it melt over a clear briuht fire, when hot, pour in the egg mixture, prick well a fork until it sets, loosen round the edge, give the pan a :shake, fold the omelet over, place on a hot dish, and serve imme- diately.

CHAPTER 1.
/24 VIZ XING'S CARL

"You will not say that, Jeanne, when you are two years older." Tall, slender Jeanne flung herself full length on the turf, and pushed her clustering hair off her face; she had a more expressive face than is usually found in a girl of thirteen. She was fair-skinned, auburn-haired, and grey-eyed. Just now she looked defiant; her large bright eves were fixed on her tall companion, who sat watching her with expectant amusement on his strong, sunburnt face. "I thought you were wise, 'Rolland • and yet you make a great mistake. You are as jar as pbasible from the truth; but then, how can a man know what a girl feels?. Two years older, indeed! Why. then I shall more than ever wish to be a boy,; I shall have to wear my gown longer, and my hair will have to be twisted up.in a tight knot under my coif; besides, there will;be a new hardship. Shall I tell you what it will be, you blind Rolland ? " She looked around her at the windows behind the plot of • grass on which she and her companion were enjoying the sunshine in the castle gardes everything seemed to be asleep, except the pigeons preening and cooing in the quaint round dove-cote at the end of the garden; there was, too, now and then a twitter among the birds in the trees right and left of the castle court, into which the garden led by a small wicket. Jeanne went on in a lowered voice, lest there should be some hidden listener; she tried to look grave, but her eyes twinkled.

"It is a. great secret, but I shall tell you, for mother always says you are to be trusted in every- thing. When two years are past I shall no longer live here; I shall be at Laval with my husband, the qount. of Laval."

Rolland de In Touche started and reddened; he opened his lips to speak, and then checked the words. Jeanne was watching the effect of her news; and she saw the red spread to the roots of his fair hair, and even under his darker beard; she saw, too, a brighter light than usual in his eyes. oiarhy do you not speak ? " she said impatiently. "I want to know what you think ? " "Do you speak in jest or in earnest, child? After to-day I may not see you again before I leave Brittany. Come, tell me, Jeanne; I must know the truth before I go to Amboise." Jeanne sprang up from the grass, her face was full of keen IntereBt, i'Amboice " she cried. "Happy you Why did you not tell me sooner you were going there? At Amboise you will see our glorious King; Gillonne calls him nogre Trai roi gaillard ' ; and you will 'also see the lady I love, though I have never seen her since she held me in her arms at my baptism; but I know how sweet she is. You know that Madame de Chateaubriand is my cousin as well as my sponsor. lam called Francoise after her." know that she is your cousin." Then, as if he wished to dismiss an unpleasant subject, "Tell me your true meaning about the Count of Laval; say that you were joking just now," he said earnestly. • She flung back her silky auburn hair till it • fell loosely on her shoulders; then leaning forward, her finger on her lips, her rounded cheek almost touch- ing his beard; "Hush! it is a secret between mother and me. Now listen: the Sing has sent his commands—you know lam the King's ward—that lam to marry Monsieur de Laval, as a reward to him for some service which he has rendered King Francis; the Count is to come very soon to Longuodec, to wed me. The pity of it is," she said, with a pathetic look in her eyes, "there is to be none of the pleasant wooing Gillonne's ballads tell about; I have no power to say Yes or No; I am to be married just like one of the dolls I used to play with ; then I am to stay here with mother till lam fifteen. But that is not all my news—oh, no. Madame de Chateaubriand has sent me her portrait set in amethysts; it is so lovely; and she sends word that some day she hopes to see me at Amboise." Ah the joy of seeing my sweet Cousin Francoise ' She began to pout. "I do not want a husband; I shall be sure to hate him. Now you see why I want to be a rdystering boy, instead of a caged-up girl. Holy Virgin! a boy is not married to a strange woman whethr he likes it or not!" She said the last words passionately, and Rolland saw tears in her bright grey eyes. "Listen, dear child "—he bad been absorbed by her news, feeling very sad—"after all, Monsieur de Laval may not want to marry you. He is a noble cad courteous gentleman; he will not thwart Madame Ilergrist if she asks for delay; our King, too, is never despotic in these contracts." Jeanne sat down again: she was pulling up the grass by tufts, which she flung across at a huge deerhound; lying basking in the afternoon sunshine. Every now and then the dog lifted his head, gazed sleepily at'his se-salient, and then settled to sleep again. "My mother does not wish for delay," Jeanne answered. "She called me to her presence seven days past and told, me she rejoiced to leave me in the hands of so good and powerful a noble as the Count de LavaL But, Rolland, Ido not like that word powerful; are you not sorry. for me ? " Her eyes again looked pathetic, and her red lips pouted out imploringly towards him, as if she sought his protection against her future husband. csAh o

Rolland rose from the grass-plot; he turned his back on Jeanne, and stood pulling his brown beard, while he looked at the château which rose above. the garden. He was a tall, well-grown, soldierly man, about fifteen years older than Jeanne; he knew the meaning of the Countess's words, and he felt sure she had not fully explained herself to the girl. Rolland's early years had been passed •at Longuedec. The Count and "Countess had treated him as though he were their own sun, and baby Jeanne had been to him as a little sister. The years went on; the young fellow fancied he was in- tended to marry his little playfellow when he came into his inheritance; his parents had died while he was yet a boy, but he had always had a happy home at Longuedec ; his strong castle of Coetfrec was a mere fortress, with little land attached to it; in a few years at most he must succeed his crippled uncle as the Lord of Orbee, a viscounty with large estates near Lisieux.

But for this certainty he would not have aspired to marriage with so wealthy an heiress as Jeanne Ke,rgrist, for -besides her father's possessions near Gitingamp she would inherit, in right of her mother, the rich and extensive landholding Of Longuedec. At Rolland's last visit, Madame Kergrist had told him in confidence that since:the Count's death Jeanne had become a ward of Ring Francis; the Countess added to this the sad tidings that she knew she had but a few years to live. Rolland looked' at the grey castle with strange discontent. He was depressed as well as discon- tented ; it was a bitter disappointment to learn that his spoilt little favourite was destined to belong to anyone but himself. He had been Jeanne's self- elected tutor in hawking and other outdoor sports; he had taught her to ride, anthhad encouraged her in all sorts of daring feats; he had also helped to form her mind by reading aloud to her and her mother, when he could find time, in the long winter evenings. Once, during the chaplain's illness, he had taught the girl some Latin. He had quitted Longuedee soon after the Count's death; but Ciietfree was within easy distance, so that his friendship for Jeanne and her mother had not slackened.

He turned again impulsively to the girl, who still sat on the grass looking at him, her slender fingers clasped round her knees. "Why was not I told about this marriage? You belong to me, Jeanne. Have not I had a hand in the making of you ?—not your flesh and bones— but I have a large part in you, Jeanne, I have helped to fashion your tastes and habits; you must always be my bright little Ptipil. It is hard to give you up. With a saucy glance from under her upward- curving lashes, she blew him a kiss; then, gather- ing her masses of straying hair, she deftly twisted up the long coil into a knot, and replaced a close- fitting white coif that lay on the grass beside her. She laughed as she sprang up and measured her height against his arm. "Not so little, my friend; see, my head nearly reaches your shoulder! I'll wager you could not carry me up the castle stairs to-day as quickly as you did last year, when you pulled me out of the river. Ah, how good you were, dear Rolland! " She lovingly patted his arm. "Yes, you ought to I, have been told about this before now. Tell me, how soon do YOU depart from C6etfrec ? "

"In seven nays. 4t.mffe,,to haft at Vonore', where orders wiliVihitst me; in that came I shall go 'on to LyOnKtind shall not visit Amboise before I leave France."' leanne shook her bead at him. "Ah, no; you 'Must go to Amboise ; you could not forego the pleasure ,Of seeing Madame de . Chateaubriand ; and it will:be unkind to disappoint me. You are so observant, you will describe to me her beauty and her dress; and—and—you will notice whether her eyes are like mine. Gillonne says they are the same colour." She hung her head and blushed at her own vanity, for she knew that Madame de Chateaubriand was considered the beauty of the Court. Rolland was silent; he stared hard at the pigeon- cote; and then he fingered the belt of his doublet. At last he turned to Jeanne. "Dear child, keep your love for your mother and *he friend* who care for it; you waste it on kadame de Chateaubriand ; she is a fair lady, but —" Hi stopped; 'prisently he added: "She does not deserve your love' Jeanne's anger made her pale. "Out upon your Malice—to speak ill of so sweet a lady! Fie lit is mean of you, Rolland! you are as hard as Gillonne ; but then, she is a woman, forced to live within castle walls, which nourish mean fancies!" The colour flew back to her cheeks as she cried out: "A man, who goes out and in as he pleases, and sees camps and cities and palaces, ought not to have carping thoughts." She had frowned a line in her smooth white forehead. "Well done, Jeanne! Bravely spoken!" He laughed; then he took both her hands, and draw- ing her close to him, in spite of her struggle to be free, he bent down and kissed her forehead. "Farewell, my little preacher; I will meditate on that text till our next meeting, for I. shall come once again, to bid adieu to the Countess, and to you also, pretty petulance. I leave you a text in return: Life may be dulled, between stone walls to bide, But it is safe ; dangers undreamed of lurk outside. But Jeanne was still angry. As soon as she could free her hands she darted through the open wicket-gate, and then across the court to the entrance door of the castle, the only entrance to the inhabited part of the building. It was protected by a drawbridge over the inner moat, Is portcullis, and all manner of defences. The only separate entrance was to the great square donjon tower behind. This door led into the inner ,block of grey stonework, which was like the outer wall of the castle, cornered by four round towers. Jeanne turned sharply to the left, and then hurried up a narrow stairway that circled round a stone newel to the top of one of the towers; slits lighted the staircase, but it smelt as musty as a granary. Jeanne passed by several doors in a long, gloomy passage. She paused at the end, raised the heavy latch of a door in the further tower, and entered a mall round chamber, with a deeply-recessed window that looked down on,the bright river beyond the outer walls. Sunshine streamed in and fell in a broad mass on the floor, but it did not reach Jeanne's little bed in one corner. A slab of stone fixed into the wall sup- ported a coarse earthenware bowl and a pitcher; two wooden stools, a prayer desk, above which hung a crucifix, a kneeling-hassock and an em- broidery frame, made the furnishing of the little chamber; there was also a dark carved-oak chest, in lieu of a wardrobe. A sprig of holly, duly blessed, was placed at the bed head, and on a small table against the grey wall was a portrait enclosed in a wooden case, while another stood up and rested against the wall itself. It was the painted portrait of a man of commanding presence, with a pale face, dark wild eyes, and a stern yet I.ttractive expression on his aquiline features; the attraction lay in the truth and purity of the face; the command in it savoured of Royal power. It was the portrait of her father's dearest friend, the Constable de Bourbon, the hero of Jeanne's childish worship. Jeanne went to the window, and looked at the river. "Rolland is unkind; it is simple cowardice to speak ill of the absent; I will never forgive him!" She suddenly laughed. "What am I doing?— crying out on Rolland, who is not here to defend himself! But then lam a featherhead of a girl, and he is a wise, strong man; he is ray friend —yes, and I have sent him away with reproaches for a keepsake."

div.head: CHAPTER IL DIA.WED.
div.p: CHAPTER IL DIA.WED.
"Mademoiselle! Mademoiselle Jeanne! A plague on the child! My wind is spent in crying after her! Where can she be hidden?"

A tall, long-faced woman, soberly dressed in black, with a white coif hiding every thread of her hair, came hurrying round the inner square of the castle to a corner of the courtyard near the donjon, where, circled in by stone walls, was the orchard. The broad-spreading apple-trees were thick with leaves, almost hidden by the rosy cloud of blossom that lay on them. Gillonne did not at first observe Jeanne's small cloth-shod feet and ankles, so near in colour was her hose to the old grey wood of the ladder placed against a blossom- covered' tree.

Gillonne was ruffled; she had gone from tower to tower in search of her young lady, and at last had sought her in the orchard, though at present there was no fruit to be found there except wild straw- berries.

"Eh—what is it, then, my poor Gillonne ? " came with a pleasant laugh out of the apple tree. "Why are you seeking me? I am but gathering a posy for my mother's table; the fruit will be the finer if ' the tree spares some of its promise." . . . .
A 'Mademoiselle must hasten! " Gillonne cried. "The Countess wearies till mademoiselle comes to her. There is stirring news for mademoiselle. come—come heedfully; it is not well to risk a fall."

This was said in protest against the speed with which Jeanne descended, one hand cumbered by a bunch of fipple-blossom. Gillonne looked admiringly at the blossom. "I need a flower wherewith to deck my bride." She smiled at the girl instead of giving the lecture Jeanne expected to receive. "A bride's attire calls for fitting blossom." She tOok-thp flowers from ,jeanne. "There seems' to be enough to deck the altar as well as the bride; pear-blossom would be more fitting, but that. is withered." "What mean you, Gillonne, by a bride ? " Jeanne looked excited; her eyes sparkled, her fieeks glowed. "Mademoiselle will learn. She must come; the Countess waits." Three doors in the gloomy passage that led to Jeanne's bedchamber opened into the Counteses• apartments. First came a large room in which She sat with her maidens; the next was her bedchamber; the furthest of all was her oratory. She now raised the heavy -tapestry that shut this off from her bedchamber, and °ante forward. .Madame Kergrist was very tall and pale, her long black robes swept the floor, but her movement was full of grace as she bent forward and kissed Jeanne's forehead.

"The time is short, dear child." Her voice was tender almost to sadness, as she looked towards the window. "I have a message from Monsieur de Laval. He and his train are riding over from. Guingamp they will be here in an hour. All is ready but you, my child. Take her, Gillonne; you shall yourself tire her. Annie will serve my turn, for I will not sadden your bridal, dear little one, with mourning weeds." She pressed Jeannie fondly to her, and then gently pushed the astonished girl towards Gillonne. Jeanne looked wide-open eyes at the shin- ing mass of white-and,silyer brocade spread out 1-.tifily on her bed. There was also a white velvet coif, sewn with Small pearls and edged with larger Imes, and this was placed over her long silky hair, .en that had been carefully made fast. by ;t.ne's practised lingers. The inner white robe fell straight and stiff from the throat, and hid her feet; Over this was a sort of peJisse, open in front, of stiff white-and-silver brocade, falling straight to the ground, cut square at the throat; with long hanging sleeves, a long veil of shimmering gauze was fastened to the cap, and made a sort of gal() round the sweet girlish face.

Gillonnejooked her charge up and down with a satisfied smTle. "The blossom is best for the chapel," she said; " 'twould mar the gown to add colour to it, and Madame has planned it herself from her portrait of the good Queen Anne. It is not the newest mode, but I have heard that our Queen Claude's bridal robe was fashioned on the same pattern." The Countess came in to see how lovely her child looked in bridal array • but time had sped fast while Gillonne performed her duties, and Madame Bergrist had only time to say a few words and to give Jeanne a fond kiss, when a summons came for madame and mademoiselle to descend to the great hall.
The old seneschal stood there, waiting to conduct them to seats placed at the further end 1 the vast

cnamner, hung with fine biue ana green tares! representing a forest, with an antlered stag in the foreground, with huntsmen and bowmen among the distant trees. Jeanne groaned inwardly under the weight of her bridal robes, but her delight in their beauty helped her to bear it • she had begun to praise them too her mother, When the seneschal again entered from the great door at the end of the hall. Beside Win I walked a keen-faced old man, the chamberlain of the Count of Laval; behind them came it group of 'pages. Jeanne watched while the seneschal marshalled them to Stand on either side of the door. • Now there came in a ge*leman of middle height and middle age, clean-shaven, and with a pleasant, debonair look on his well-featured face; a taller, much younger man walked beside him. As the girl met his narrow bright eyes fixed on her,, they reminded her of the eyes of a snake. He was both handsome and graceful, and yet Jeanne shivered with a dread that this younger man might be her destined husband.

The Countess bent her head in gracious welcome; she held out her hand to the elder gentleman. He bent and kissed it; then craved leave to present his young cousin, Etienne de Retz. Jeanne had never seen such ceremonious bows and curtseys as were now interchanged, and she took a child's delight in the stateliness of her mother's reception; it seemed to make her marriage far more important and interesting than she bod expected it to be. When her mother presented her the Count of Laval smiled pleasantly at his little bride. "I had fancied your daughter was older, madame," he said, when he had kissed the slender, childish hand; "she scarcely looks twelve years old."

Jeanne longed to say: "I am almost thirteen," but she knew she must not speak unless she was spoken to. Monsieur de Retz, however, saw her indignant eyes, and gave her a significant smile. Jeanne looked away; she tried to listen to the talk between her mother and the Count, but some . irresistible power brought her eyes again to the handsome, sneering face, and to the eyes that bad an uncanny attraction for her. ' The Count of Laval had brought his chaplain, and the two priests and their server stood ready to receive the wedding-party ,as it proceeded to the chapel, on the same floor with the hall. ' It all seemed like a dream to Jeanne when the ring was placed on her finger; she longed to rub her eyes to make sure she was awake. Then she saw the clusters of apple-blossom in the altar vases. "I must be awake,' she thought; "only a while ago I plucked those flowers." She knelt beside her bridegroom to receive the priest's blessing. A few rninutea later she found herself with him in the sacristy. While the Count was signing the register a voice whispered in Jeanne's ear: "The sacrifice is too great; the victim is too fair and young; my heart bleeds to witness such cruelty. Jeanne raised her head and looked steadfas. tly into De Retz's eyes. "There can be no sacrifice, monsieur, where there is good-will." She signed her name after the Count's, and she felt a sense of safety when he drew her cold fingers into his warm grasp and led her from the chapel. _
(To be continued.)

div.head: SUNSET.
div.p: SUNSET.
Fast fading from oar raptured view, In clouds of gold and crimson hue . . ,

Day's circling orb,with glory crowned. Now lingers on his empire's bound : More mild, more lovely still, and pleased the while To see the quiet world responsive smile. And Eve, sweet maid, so calm, an ehr, With noiseless step and pensive ere, Comes forth on hill and lonely dell, To breathe a balmy, soft farewell ; And westward twles her gaze that she may share The wondrous vision that surrounds him there. But fainter now that vision grows, Nearer the gloomy shadows close ; A little while—'twill all be o'er, And yon red aim be E0(11 no more, Till morn again unveils the kindling skies, And bids him in new light and glory rise. Farewell awhile, thou setting sun,>.. We, too, another stage have run Like thee through storm and cloud have ' To reach a peaceful goal at last (ass d, And thouv,h elf-Willed at times and apt to roam. We love the hand tnat gently leads us home_ -- Our twilight hues all lowly seem. But evanescent as a dream ; No ling'ring ray, no streak of light May reach the grave's dark starless night. Where we ere long, unknowing and unknowu, Shall fill ocr niche among the dead alone. Von setting sun will rise at morn To freshened power and glory born ; And we like him would sink to rest With calm unshrinking faith pospess'd In Tim whose footsteps made the grave's dark wa7 Tbe path that leads to everlasting day. J. H. W. CLINDINNING.

THE DREDGING OPXRATIONS. The report of the navigation of the river Merest in 1897 to the Commissioners for the Conservancy 01 the River, by Vice Admiral Sir G. S. Nurse, actiog conservator, has just been published. Alluding t° the Manche3ter Ship Canal, the report says :--" Th? Conservancy has been informed by the officers oi• the Manchester Ship Canal Company that during the year 1897 no dredging operations were carried on in the Mersey estuary at the Bromborough end of the approach channel to the canal, but 163,00°, tons of silt were raised from. the &fathom end 01 that channel immediately below Eastham locks during the year and deposited at sea. From the reaches of the Mersey between Messrs. Monks' Hall's works at Bank Quay, Warrington. and the lock at Howley Weir 163,407 tons of material were raised and deposited oit land beyond the reach of the highest tido; From the length of the canal between Eastbam an.° Latchford 650,532 tens of silt were dredged. div.head: LIFE IN THE CHEMICAL METROPOLIS. wIDNEs MAN'S REMARKABLE STATEMENT.
div.p: LIFE IN THE CHEMICAL METROPOLIS. wIDNEs MAN'S REMARKABLE STATEMENT.

Nicch has been written about the terrible lot Of the " white slaves" of Widnes. Thrilling descriptions have been given, with more or leis lurid colouring,of the dan- gers through which they have to pass to win their daily bread,aed soul-depressing pictures have been drawn as to their homes and the manner in which they spend their leisure hours. The work was well done to create a sensation,but it was grotesquely overdrawn as a picture of what life in the chemical metropolis really is, even in the alkali works. You would not imagine so from the articles written by London literary gentlemen, but it is a fact that in many of the Widnes chemical works, sur- rounded by chimneys, furnaces, " revolvers," and salt- cake pans, beautiful plants are grown,in which consider- able pride is taken, and within a stone's throw of " waste "heaps, flourishing corn crops are now grow- ing. Wllnes, however, is not given over entirely to the manufacture of chemicals. It is famed for other indus- tries, one of which is the production of soap,,and its manufacture finds employment for close on a thousand man and boys. In some of its departments the work is exhausting, especially in the hot summer weather, though not too heavy, and taken as a whole the opera- tives are a strong, healthy body of men. In rase of sickness, however, at Messrs. Gossige's works, admir- able provision is made for those who are temporarily disabled in life's battle' and through the medium of the Werke Club, skilful medical attendanc 3 is at the service of those who are stricken down. But how often do we find that the physician fails to stop the advance of an insidious disease. A remarkable case of this descrtption hasjust been i,rrquired into by a reporter of the •••• 'Widnes Weekly News.

Mg, %Milan Jones. IMr. William Jones, whose portrait illustrates -this art:6N has now passed the meridian of life. Born at Llandulas, a pretty village on the North Wales coast,47 years ago, like many of his countrymen he wended his way into Lancashire, and he now resides at 20, White. street, Widnes. For the past 20 years he has waited for Means. W. Gossage and Sons, hia occupation for the past four years having been that of a soapboiler. Up to about two years ago he had never known a day's Sic*. ness. He had always been fit for a day's work. Then his troubles commenced. Interviewed by the Pressman, he said : " It was about two months before Christmas, 'E6, , when I went on the club, but I had not been in good I health for a considerable time before that. I bad severe Irains in the stomach, and they became so acute that I had to leaie my work. I went to the doct.Gr, who it I was suffering from indigestion. He gave me medicine, but it did me no good. I then consulted another prac- titioner. He said, at first, that it was indigestion, but afterwards be said be was afraid there was something forming internally. I had now been off work two weeks, and the prospect was looking gloomy. So I went to Liverpool, and consulted an eminent specialist, and he to'd me that was suffering from a sluggish stomach and enlargement of the liver. He gave me a prescription. and after another week I was able to resume work. I went to the specialist every fortnight or three weeks for .four months, hot thaugh I followed his prescriptions regularly the pains continue ialmo4 uaabated. Sin'- times I felt better and sometimes worse, and he: kept changing the medicine in a manner I could not under- stand. Owing to the expense I ceased my visits for three or four months but I contintrd taking his medicine. The P 1 n then got worse and I c linmenced going to the specialist as before, and kept it up for another three mouths. The pains were now so severe that I was scarcely able to work. It was at this time that I happened to see a pamphlet describing Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. I read it with interest and was glad to see that these pills had cured people who had suffered from exactly the same complaint as I was the victim of. The same night I wrote to Dr. Williams' Company, stating my case, and I received a prompt reply advising me to try the pills. About else same time a lady friend from Runcorn., visited us and she told us that the pills had done her husband, who suffered from paralysis, a great deal of rood. lat once Is might a box and commenced taking them, and an improvement in my condition Was soon manifested. I took them regularly after meals, as prescribed, add after takinr three or four boxes I began to feel better. I commenced taking them on iegust 16th last year, and in about a fortnight the swelling, in the stomath and the attendant pains began to disappear. Altogether I took several boxes of the pills before 1 was thoroughly better." "How do you keel now 9" asked the reporter. 4.1 was never better. and if I am never worse I shah net die from illness. The pains and the depression of apirits they caused have gone enbirely. I still take one of the pills new and •,eain, because I have great confid- ence in them. lam sure it was the pills that cured me, or I would not recommend them to anyone else. No- thing did me any good until I commenced taking the Pills, and I feel thankful for such a remedy." "Have you any objection to your statement being pub- Ilished?" " None whe.tever. I have said nothing but what I am willing to stand by, and I should like other people who suffer like I have done to know of this cure.' Mrs. Jones and her daughters who were present dur- ing the interviow. were equally emphatic as to the cau.e of Mr. Jones' cure, and remarked that for many months past he was in continual pain but ha S now im- proved in appearance and health wonderfully.

There have been a nuoaber of rumours in circula- tion recently with regard to toe relations between Franco and lorocco, and particularly in reference to the possible action of France in taking possession of the Saharan oases that lit to the south-west of Algeria. There has been the usual oliicial denial that any serious action is in contemplation, but private advices from El Golea practically places it beyond all reasonable doubt that the Governor General of Algeria is making arrangements for extending French influence over these oases. Indeed, it is said that the occupation of these oases will "certainly be an accomplished fact this autumn." Tbe expedition which is to effect this will be led by Commandant Godron, and as a preliminary step the chiefs of a religious order which has great influence with the tribes of the Sahara have been given posts in the local administration. It is doubtful, how- ever, if the resistance which the Tuaregs are cer- tain to offer will be very materially lessened by these tactics. These desert warriors will have the great advantage of an intimate knowledge of the country; and, as the French have already learnt by bitter experience, they are past-masters of the ambuscade. How far these operations will affect the relations of France with Morocco it is impos- sible to predict, but they certainly contatn the seeds el possible complications.

Electrical engineers are taking the keenest inter- est in a scheme, now before a committee of the I House of Lords, for the supply of electrical energy to manufacturers. Similar schinies have been in successful operation for some time in Germany and America, but so far as this country is concerned the proposal is a novelty. The promoters, who are men of substance and high ilnandal position, are prepared to guarantee a capital of a million ster- ling. Their plans involve the construction of great generating works at a place called Warsop, near 1 Mansfield, from which they propose to supply an area of 2,000 square miles. They believe that all kinds of works would gladly take advantage ot the •economical and ready-made power in which they desire to deal. Even the smallest of cottage indus- tries, they say, might be expected to benefit from a scheme which would put electricity within reach of the humblest purse. While no one questions the feasibility of the enterprise, it is meeting with the determined opposition of a number of munici- palities, including Sheffield, Nottingham, Chester- field,and Lincoln,all of whom seem to be contem- plating independent schemes of a similar nature.

The War Office will be called upon before long to defend the indulgence it has extended to thedfficers implicated in the Jameson raid. Generally speaking the House will take alenient view of what the War Office has done, but its action will be impugned in a searching and cynical criticism by Mr.Labouchere. Officers who have been guilty of misconduct are not when called upon to retire, entitled to certain al- lowances and gratuities which are granted to officers who have not been guilty of any misconduct. That the Jameson officers were guilty of a gross breach of duty goes without saying, and the deci- sion of the War Office to grant them the forbidden allowances has been condemned by the Committee on Public Accounts. This condemnatien does not annul the grant, but it exposes the War Office to criticism, and puts it on its defence. It will be in- teresting to see by what gloss it overcomes the ex- press language of the warrant relating to compul- sory retirement.

The Petroleum Committee has by no means done with its work, though it has come to a decision Upon the flash-point. Mr.Collings's recommendation about lamps were founded on the idea that the flash-point of 73 degrees would be retained,and that the evidence all went to show that the majority of the accidents arose from dangerous lamps. He held to this notion with a dogged tenacity, notwith- standing Lord Kelvin's view, and felt fortified by his opinion being also that of the late Sir Vivian Majendie. Now a Government official is very diffi- cult to reasen out of any notion he has once taken up. As Mr. Collings stands on cheap oil for the poor, he will, when the question of framing a Bill CO9lOB on, either adhere to the 73 degrees which he favours, or compromise by the adoption of some standard between 73 and 100. The narrow majority by which 100 degrees was adopted indicates that the Government will only carry its point by the force of party discipline.

The occupation of the Liao-To-Shan lighthouse by the Russians places the lighting of the entrance of the Gulf of Fechili absolutely in their hands. So at least say Mr. Yerburgh and his.lriends of the "Far East Committee." Consequently-they propose "to take further action in the matter." The Com- mittee are also anxious that our Government should offer a guarantee in aid of the construction of rail- ways by British capitalists in China. Mr. Yerburgh reports a strongleeling in the Noath -of England in favour of the adoption f such a policy by Her Majesty's Government. The Bill which produces a revolution in connec- tion with the evidence in criminal cocoa, and per- mits accused persons to give evidence, and which is to go before a committee of the whole House,runs the risk of being drowned in llolds of legal talk. Seldom, if ever, base Bill so rousel the pugnacity of the legal section of the House. All the lawyers want to speak upon it every time it is called, and the speeches are of fatiguing length. This makes its prospects in Committee doubtful, and the only hope of its passing lies in the fact that it is short. Mr. Balfour' s back is stiff upon the subject at pre- sent, and if it remains so the Attorney General will get the measure through. The lawyery in the House are about equally divided for and against it, and party politics do not come into the reckoning. So little is this the case that Mr. A=quith and Mr. J Morley took completely opposing lines last night, the one rising immediately after the other to to answer his arguments, to the great amusement of all parties, and even of the Front Opposition Bench itself.

Sir William Harcourt has not retreated from his position on Romanising Ritualism, as has been in- sinuated in some quarters, and he returned to the subject on Tuesday, on the third reading of the Benefices Bill,in a speech quite as firm and resolute but less fiery and denunciatory than those of last week. He freed himself from ambiguity,hoth by the line of argument he adopted and by the extra- ordinary temperateness of his language and style of speech. His argument comes simpl y to this, that the organised attempt which is being made by a large body ot clergy to identify the doctrines and practices of the Church of England with th *se of the Church of Rome should have been dealt with by the Bill, or that clergy who feel the ,obligations of their ordination vows too onerous and irksome should leave the Church -It will not be possible for his opponents to find fault with what he has said for the whole exposition of his attitude was a studied and successful eflf )rt in moderation. Scarcely a strong phrase escaped him. If he had drawn as firm and clear a line of demarca- tion round his position from the first,be would have eseaped much misunderstanding.

There is evidently very great interest in the question of the financial relations between Great Britain and Ireland among the Irish public authorities. A return which has been prepared shows that petitions to the House of Commons on the subject have been adopted and sealed by seven corporations, 70 bodies of town commissioners, six chambers of commerce, 101 poorlaw unions, 16 asylum boards and 11 bodies of harbour commis- sioners ;in all '2ll public bodies. This is by no means without interest in view of the forthcoming debate.

• The c3ustnittee of Service members are rather jubilant at having shaken Mr. Goschen out of his official ruts in reference to his shipbuilding pro- gramme ; and the assurances they have given hiss, that they will support any addition to the flees that he may propose whieh will maintain the absolute naval supremacy of the country, is quite superflu- ous. They will exert themselves to make his new programme as large as possible, but it would be too glaring an admission of official blundering if Mr. Goschen met them evren half-way. If he wants to i` sleep o' nights" during the rest of his adminis- tration at the Admiralty, he may as well take the whole leap at one bound, for the demands upon him nest year will be as urgent,and, in feet, insur- gent, as they have been this.

A fire resultinc in the destruction of cotton valued at nine laktis of rupees has occurred at Bombsy. - At Winchester As.izes on Wednesday. Alice Robinson was sentenced to death for strangling her eleven months old child at Fareham

A Trornso telegram statei that lidr. Walter Wellman, the American explorer, left there on 'Monday on board his ice steamer Frithyof, for the North Polar regions. A telegram from Nijni Novgorod reports a great conflagra- tion in the quarter of the town situated beyond the Kama river, 100 dwelling-houses being reduced to ashes. Carrara. the mushroom grower who murdered a Paris bank manager last February, was guillotined at daybreak on Saturday morning, before the gates of Roquette Prison. The swimming race for the Northern Count,es 1.000 yards championship took place at Rochdale on Saturday. and was won by P. Lister. Derbyshire was only able to take third place.

LOCAL PARISH COUNCIL
MEETINGS. STOCKTON HEATH.

On Tuesday evening a meeting of the Parish Counci of Stockton Heath was held in the National schoolroom. Mr. Mason presided, and there were also present Mr. J. Mclntyre, Mr. J. H. Clarke, with Mr. E. Bradshaw (clerk),
THE SUGGESTED IMPROVEMENT OPPOSITE THE POST OFFICE.

Mr. Mclntyre informed the Council that the deputa- tion appointed to wait upon Mr. Vera Davies did so,but It was found that he was not the trustee. He gave them the name,but at present they were not in a position to make any statement about the matter.—The Chairman: What land do you refer to ?—Mr. Mclntyre : The land Opposite the Post Office.

_ _ THE EE-PLAEING OP PUBLIC SEATS. The Clerk remarked that be had written to Mr. Pem- berton about the seats.—Mr. Clarke: They are much appreciated by the public.—The Chairman: People liv- ing in London-road and Red-lane are dissatisfied, but I told one gentleman who complained that he had no locus stands.—Mr. Mclntyre: Are the seats fixed firmly ? The one at London Bridge you could shake; it was very loose indeed. If the iron seat is fixed in the same way it will be off the road altogether.—The Chairman : The two at the bridge here appear to be all right.—The sub- ject then dropped.

div.head: TEN -COST OF TEE RE'IENT ELECTION.
div.p: TEN -COST OF TEE RE'IENT ELECTION.

The Clerk submitted a number of accounts for pay- ment. One account was that of Mr. Ashton, the clerk to the Rural Council, for £l3 lOs 71, the cost of the contested elections in the township in 1898.—The Clerk pointed out that the Parish Council paid half the account, and the Rural District Council the other.—Mr. Clarke : The elections have cost the ratepayers a half- penny in the 4.—The accounts were passed.
WALTON GRININ.

The Clerk called the attention of the Council to the fact that the fence round Walton Green was badly knocked about. The tree was aleo dead.—Mr. Clarke said there were some good trees on the Brewery ground which were about to be pulled down. He thought he would be able to get one for the Council if the members so desired.—Mr. Clarke was instructed to use his endea- vours in that direction.—Mr. Clarke also gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the resolu- tion of the previous Council with reference to the erec- tion of hurdles be rescinded.

div.head: VOLUNTEER FIRE BRIGADE.
div.p: THE VOLUNTEER FIRE BRIGADE.

- Mr. Clarke said that volunteer firemen were wanted for the parish. They had already got one or two. The fire appliances would be in their places in a few days Two or three men had given in their names as volunteer firemen, and they hoped shortly to have the full num- ber of six. This concluded the business. GRAPPENHALL.

On Monday evening the quarterly meeting of the rappenhall Parish Council was held in the schoolroom. There were present i—Mr. A. L. Kaye (chairman), and Messrs. R. Boardman, S. M. Houghton, F. Ellison, J. Bradford, T. Smith, J. Warburton, W. Lomas, J. .1. Fairhurst, and B. J. Woodcock (clerk)—The Clerk said that at a previous meeting he was instructed to write to the Main Roads Committee of the Cheshire County Coun- cil about the passage across the Latchford Locks. The matter was held over from the last meeting,but he wrote to Mr. Reginald Potts, clerk to the County Council, to the effect that it was decided that this Council call the attention of the Main Roads Committee to the dangerous and unprotected footway across the locks. The matter had been brought before the Rural District Council, who had written to the Ship Canal Company, but it had bad no effect. They passed a resolution to the effect that they would make the Canal Company properly protect the locks.—The Chairman : They have rescinded that. He saw in the paper that the Rural District Council had refused to take any further steps in the matter. Since then, unfortunately, there had been another death. Should they leave the matter for the present, and see what steps the County Council took? They had done their best, and had said they held the Canal Company responsible for future damage. He thought the only thing to do was to wait and see what the County Council did.—lt was decided to defer the consideration of the matter for a short time.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.

In the absence of Mr. Wright, the chair at the meeting of Great Sankey Parish Council was taken on Monday evening by Mr. T. Balton. There were also present— Mr. George Thompson, Mr. William Taylor and Mr. Joseph smith (clerk).

div.head: NEGLECTED FOOTPATH.
div.p: A NEGLECTED FOOTPATH.

---- Mr. G. Thompson, ia accordance with notice of motion, moved that the attention of toe Lancashire County Council be called to the state of the footpath from Sankey Bridges to Great Sankey Board Schools. He said he felt very strongly on the matter as nothing was being done. The footpath was in a very bad con- dition, and after a shower of rain it was unfit to walk upon. He thought the footpath was used more than any ther in the aistrict. It was a footpath connected with a main road, and if the County Council knew it was in its present state he was of opinion they would take steps to put it right.—The Chairman said he quite agreed with the remarks which had been made,and admitted that the footpath was in a bad con- dition. The matter had been mentioned to the members of the Highway Board. At the same time the road was a county road.—The Clerk : lam not sure whether the Highway Board are responsible as a secondary party. Possibly they are responsible to the County Council for the condition of the toad.—The Chairman : That is a fac,and the Highway Board are paid for keeping the main roads in repair.—Mr. Thompson said the Highway Board did not seem dii•posed to move in the matter. He also alluded to the necessity of a footpath being made in front of South View. Toe new property there was of a valuable character.—The Chairman suggested that the clerk should write to the Highway Board, a suggestion which Mr. Thompson accepted. It was then decided to instruct'. the Clerk to write to the Highway Board calling their attend in to both matters.

div.head: PARISH BOX.
div.p: THE PARISH BOX.
On the proposition of Mr. Tirmnpion, it was decided that the Chairman, Vice-chairman and Clerk, be em- powored to purchase a box he which to preserve par Lia documents.
UGGESTF.I) TRIENNIAL ELECTION OF PARISH COUNCILLORS.

Mr. Thompson said he gave notice at the last meeting that he would move a resolution with reference to parish councillors continuing in office for three years instead of one year, thus saving the expense of the recurring elections.—The Chairman thought it would be advisable to leave the matter over until a fuller Board attended,as the question was an important one.—Mr. Thompson expressed his willin:iness to do so,and the subject will be iotrodined at a future meeting. 'ANOTHER PDLLUTED imom AT SANKEY. . . _

The Chairman called the attention of the Council to the condition of a brook at Sankey, which, he said, was very bad—ii fact from what he could gather the nuis- ance emanated from one source, the cutting of the new colliery at Bold.—Mr. Thompson understood that tho water front Bold was very pure.— file Chairinan did not think so. At the presennt time his men had to draw water Iron the well and put it in a large tub for the cattle to drink. Mr. Kilihaw was acting in a similar maaner. The water seemed to be polluted with a reddish material. —Toe Clerk said he also understood that the water from the Bold Colliery was exceptionally good.—Mr. Taylor remarked teat the water varied a grat deal. It was polluted from time to time. There were times when it was claar.—The Clerk suggested that he should bo in- structed to write to the Rural District Council about the matter,and they could state the facts of the case to the proprietors of the Bold Colliery.—Eventually it was de- cided that the Chairman should bring the matter under the notice of the District Council.—The Clerk : If the , Rural District Council do not take action in the matter YOU can appeal to the County Council.—Mr. Thompson: If they decline to act we can call a special meeting. It is a very important matter. IMPORTANT TO GAS CONSUMERS. The Chairman said he wished, through the press, to inform gas consumers that since the extension of the borough, consumers living within one mile from any part of the extension, were allowed to have gas at a cheaper rite than those who lived beyond the one mile radius._, Mr. Thompson : I think tbe present price is 3. The Chairman Chairman : I know gentlemen in Sankey who are paving 43. 41.—Mr. Thompson : But there is an abate- ment if the account is paid within a month.—The Clerk : Is the reduction permanent p—The Chairman : I under- stand so. I know of one resident who has seen Mr: 'taylor, the gas collector, on the Subject, and I Under- stand that all residents within the mile radius are en- titled to the return of the money overpaid since the ex- tension of the borough.—Mr.Thampson thought it would be a good thing if there could be a uniform rate. (Hear, hear.)—The Chairman also intimated that the Corpora- tion intended to extend the water mains aloag Chapel- lane, This concluded the busincsa.

PROFESSOR BARLOW'S BENEFIT AT WARRINGTON BATHS. BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCH OF THE WARRINGTON SWIMMER.
MISS LOBEL RIGBY, 84, ERIDCMSTREBT, WARRIN4TON,
BOUQUETS, SPRAYS,

It has always been the Englishman's boast that be has in his veins, the blood of the Norsemen, those hardy warriors who settled on our coasts long ago. Those sea-kings were far more at home on the water than on land and it is due to our blood and the fact that water plays such an important part in our commercial dealings that we pride our- selves on being the first maritime nation of the world. Under these circumstances swimming should be recognised as our national accomplish- ment, rather than as a pleasurable pastime. It should be a necessary part of every child's educa- tion, and more so as we know that regular bathing goes a long way towards giving health and strength. Swimming was never so popular as it is at the present time. Its popularity has been attained through the erection of swimming baths in all the large boroughs and cities and the formation of swimming clubs, competitions, and championships. Warrington can boast of swimming baths which will compare favourably with the best in the country and it is but fitting that it should be the birth-place of men of ability as swimmers. Amongst the latter who claim Warrington as their nativel town one name stands to the fore, and to the best swimmers of his day he proved a most formidable competitor. We refer to Mr. G. A. Barlow. The Manager of the Warrington Baths was born on the 26th April, 1868. Mr. Barlow is thus 30 years of age, the time of life when the athlete should possess the vitality of youth, and the full vigour of manhood. The Professor who is rather below the average height, possesses a physique indicating great muscular power and robustness. He was ap- prenticed as a whitesmith under his father, John Barlow, of Beamont-street. He first learned swim- ming in the Warrington bath and Professor Pamph- ling, of London, gave him his first lessons in the natatory art. After a little practice, he entered for his first swimming race at New Brighton in 1882. Mr. Barlow has swum in many races and won numerous prizes. In fact he was successful in every race he swam in for twelve months. Professor Bar- low (as he is sometimes called),is the only swimmer in England who has beaten Joey Nuttall,the present champion of the world, three times in amateur championship races. The first occasion was in this Isle of Man in a 100 yards open scratch race. The second occasion was at Pendleton at the opening of ; the new baths there in a 200 yards race. The third occasion was at Rochdale, for the 150 yards cham- pionship of Great Britain. In all Mr. Barlow has swum with Nuttall about eight times, always starting level,and to beat the champion in three of these races is an honoar which in its accomplishment means fast travelling. In 1885 Mr. Barlow SWhCa at Ashton-under-Lyne tor the 500 yards championship of Lancashire. There were four competitors includ- ing H. H. Britain,who had won the championship of the Mersey the same year,and had twice won the 500 yards championship race for Lancashire. Had Britain been successful on this occasion the cup (value 15 guineas) would have become his own pro- perty. Unfortunately for him he was defeated by the Warringtonian. Mr. Barlow told Britain on the I night of the competition at Ashton,that he(Barlow) was sure to beat him, when Britain replied that lie would not be one of the first three. But the result proved that Barlow had not exaggerated his powers. Britain gave in at the seventh length, eight lengths, shoe; of the accomplishment of his task, Barlow winning by the length of the batb,3o yards. Ms last occasion on which be swam in a race was about six years ago. It was a 200 yards open handicap at the Osborne-street Baths, Manchester, and it was the occasion of Nuttall's benefi!;. Mr. Barlow conceded a start of 22 seconds to Professor A. Robinson, of Leeds, and was beaten by about A yard for first prize. Mr. Barlow's stroke always attracted much atten- tion,as it was a mixture of the breast and over-arm, and what is now known as the " trudgeon "stroke. It is the opinion of many Warrington swimmer, had Mr. Barlow received proper training when he he was in active competition in swimming races,he would have done himself better justice. The otner swimmers had the ad vantage of proper training,and generally speaking, did not follow any regular em- ployment. Mr. Barlow on the other hand worked regularly and had no systematic course of training. Often he competed in championship races without changing in the least his regular mode of living.

SIR E, GREY is right in mrthg in gesting thlt we are much is" fluenced by myths in politic:4p especially at the time of a General Election.
