The retention of the punishment is t cated by officials on the ground that it is gr iu protection to the warder:, and very effie"°i°3so. the subjugation of coarse and mutinous prison. °art It appears, however, that in our convict Prls,rbe the cases of flogging are comparatively few' isic to wardert are armed, and they are usually a"
I

Protect themselves against grave assaults. It is in the local prisons that flogging is more fre- quently administered, for infractions of the prison rules. But this statement must be made with limitations. There is no flogging in Scotch and Irish prisons; consequently it cannot be contended that it is an indispensable part of Prison discipline. Yet it is to be admitted that there will be cases in which this brutal punish- may be necessary—that is, in dealing with brutes. We fear that there is no avoiding this limited statement. Prison officials are pretty unanimous in England on the point. But the fre- quency with which flogging is administered to prisoners who are under duress for light terms of IroPrisonment, and for minor offences, suggests that it has been practised much more light- iteartedly than it need be. Hence the prison re- formers say that the prisoner ought to be tried for 841 offence before he is flo.gged,and that some record aught to be kept of the evidence tendered in sup- Port of the charge against him. The Home Secre- tary offers certain improvements, but they do not seem to go far enough for the more humane re- formers, whose general contention is this—that flagging for an offence in prison which would not Warrant the punishment for a like offence outside the prison, according to the law of the land, is bad Policy. Sir HENRY Fowinft takes this view. Ob- viously, if the punishment is to be kept 'under restraint some newer regulations are required, and a prison governor ought not to be armed with a power which is not at the command of a judge in a similar case. Then Comes the other side of the question: DJO3 the Punishment have a good moral effect ? To answer this question we want to know whether offences of the like nature against prison rules are more corn- Ulon in English than in Scotch and Irish prisons ?If they are, in spite of flogging, we may have doubts aS to its efficacy. The administration of such a Punishment for any but the most violent conduct is indefensible, and there can be no doubt that if the power to award it were limited, and fenced about with restrictions, it would be much less fre- quent. Though we are unable to say that it should be absolutely abolished in all prisons, we have doubts as to its efficacy in the large majority Of cases,and doubts as to the justice of it.o ur prison system is probably more cruel than that of any other civilised country in the world, and floggina 15 one of the lingering superstitions of the official incli taking the place that hanging used to oc euPY in former times. We have restricted ha Ilging to murder, and we shal: do well to restrict °gging to the very worst of crimes a prisoner can e°ll:trait• There are many other ways of teaching a brute in prison that ho is under restraint, and if they are effective enough in other countries we do not see why E. they should not be effective in ngland, The question of flogging for special crimes, when ordered by a judge, after trtal, is quite another matter, which we do not now intend te discuss.

This evening (Friday) the Weston Parish Conn- will have under consideration the question of the Proposed new road from Runcorn to Weston. What the result of their deliberations will be, is dcult to surmise; but we hope that the question will be judged in an impartial spirit. We say lin- Partial, because there is an opinion fully expressed by the olr tai,hca t Runcorn alone will be benefited and even then only a very few Run- Prn storekeepers, who have increased facilities or taking their stores into Weston and returning with the Westonian hard cash. When such sub- jects as these enter into a question they are apt to do a lot of harm and precious little good. The road question is one that should be considered without bias, and the point is, will it do any good? Will it do any good either to Runcorn or to Weston, or perchance to both? And to these queries there can be only one fair answer. It will benefit tuncorn ; it cannot harm Weston, but it will teud to prevent the Weston shopkeepers charging luiusual prices, and securing a monopoly. There- !ore the plea for the road is a ju3tifiable one. As for the question of obtaining land, a determined rarish Council acting with unanimity can de onders in overcoming such obstacles. Whatever liar/pens we don't think any Parish Council would us Justified in dealing with a matter of this kind Without serious, thorough, and calm deliberation. The policy of haste is beyond doubt a poor policy t▪ o adopt in anything and particularly in road ulaking; and though the only perfect way is to Plan out your road and build it, as did the notaans,irrespective of property-owners,still there should be no difficulty in the accomplishment of the project when property-owners are brought to Be the value of being in the neighbourhood of a good, and well-chosen thoroughfare.

Twelve months have passed since the loyal subjects of the Queen in every part of the world Wit.sre rejoicing over the completion of her FI:?,!PY s reign of sixty years. At that celebra- , there were the beginnings of a new-born affac- ion is Loth in the colonies and the mother country. E had regarded the other with more or less Pect, but the regard had grown rather cool. er Majesty's Diamond Jubilee, however, turned the eyes of the colonies homeward, and their hearts followed. A wave of fraternity and patriot- isin swept through the British Empire and the one great yearning was to be drawn closer together, to stand by each other in times of prosperity as well as adversity, and to make the world under- stand that the British race was united by senti- taerit as well as by language. The new spirit has grown stronger and has proved not to be a blare passing whim. The pledges of loyalty remain and will be kept sacred. During the past Year we have had many instances that demonstrate h, ow sincere were the professions of true brother- need which came from our own kinsmen across t,he seas. Englishmen realised last year, perhaps for the first time, how vast were our possessions, Low varied in colour and race were the subjects of -sker Majesty, and how great the power of the tritish race might become if united and loyal. The colonists went home understanding us better, 4rid we parted with them with a feeling that they were members of one and the same family. Their return home has not diminished their enthusiasm Or lessened their desire to continue th, good work Which they pledged themselves to carry out while they were participating in the festivities of the jubilee.

-- There seems every probability that one of the foullest blots on our criminal law will be removed 911 ring the present session of Parliament,and that ;s the prohibition of prisoners, or their wives or husbands from giving evidence. The Bill to grant privilege—which we can hardly imagine any rair-minded person opposing—was discussed in c'lrirnittee of,the House of Commons on Wednesday afternoon, when there were indications of the peasure passing into law before very long. Though the advantages and justice of the Bill seem patent on the face of it,there are some members of Parlia- liltient who show great unwillingness to assent to s ratification. Those are mostly comprised In the legal section of the House, one argument

advanced by them being that the prisoner electing to take the oath and give evidence on his own be- half will be liable to such cross-examination by counsel or Judge as would tend to convict him out of his own mouth, even, may be, when inno- cent. We can frankly say that this reason is not one that appeals to us with way weight. It is too much to suppose that prosecuting counsel would be so devoid of any sense of fairness, and so influ- enced by a desire to secure conviction that they 'would badger the unfortunate prisoner into admis- sion' tantamount to guiltiness. The stron,ges argument in favour of this reformation in criminal administration is the anomaly of a prisoner's wife being able to "swear" against him in a court of justice,but being precluded from giving evidence on his behalf. The same rule of course is applicable to the husband when his wife is the prisoner. To mete out justice is what the cases are tried for, and while the present absurd system is in vogue it is impossible for an abso- lutely just decision to be arrived at in cases where the evidence is insufficient or questionable.

The East B.erts election result is one of those which may be called a moral victory if not an actual win: There have been several such events since the present Government entered upon its tenure of office, and these, coupled with the numerous out-and-out victories which have been recorded on the side of Liberalism, cannot be looked upon as anything else but an unmis- takeable indication that the tide which flowed the way of the Unionists in 1895, has turned and is now unswervingly sweeping onward to an ultimate Liberal triumph. East Herts, though still a Con- servative constituency, has revealed such a meta- morphosis in the composition of its electorate, that the supporters of the Govern- ment are not unnaturally filled with apprehension. Mr. Cecil, a nephew of the Prime Minister, was a strong car didate, but instead of maintaining the triumphs of his predecessors he by a mqjority of 255. ,:ls go ertvhatoirtvlee " Party were able to gloat In nas 18920 nlytt s et over a margin of 1458, while at the last general electio,l they were left in undisputed possession of the Ii Id. Such facts as these make a startling comnientary on the hold which the supporters of the Government possess on the feelings of the g , nation. That hold is decreasing as steadily as the principles of Liberalism are findin wider and wider acceptance, and the cause for it, in the main, ' is etuhte. ever-growing unpopularity of the Govern-

A considerable amount of time was spent at the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians last week in discussing the recommendation of the Officers' Committee that an increase of wages be given to the baker, engineer and barber An- ployod at the Workhouse. It is true that the dis- cussion waged chiefly around the question whether the newlv-formed Officers' Committee had power to submit such recommendations as a separate committee, but still the attitude of some members in opposing the it.crease of wages on economical grounds seemed to be that of straining at a gnat whilst willing to swallow a camel. The total in- crease of wages proposed for the three employs in question amounts to £lB per annum,or about seven shillings weekly between the three men. Now it may he readily z,npoosed—judging from previous experience of local authorities—that if the pro- posal had loam one of increasing a prominent offi- cials salary by such 4i round sum as say £2O or even £5O per annum it would have been agreed to with less demur than the few shillings weekly for the three minor employs alluded to.

It is only a few weeks since Warrington was assured of the determination of the Lancashire County Council to put an end to the nuisance of Sankey Brook by.cornpelling the St. Helens Cor- poration to deal with the sewage which they daily put into it. A petition was presented by the County authority against the Si. Helens Corpora- tion Bill, now before Parliament, with the object of obtaining a clause to compel the St. Helens Corporation to deal with the subject, and it really looked as if the Lancashire County Council meant what they said. They have now withdrawn their opposition to the St. Helens Bill simply because the St. Helens Corporation have written them a letter promising to deal with the sewage emptied into Sankey Brook within two years. Such an undertaking carries with it no legal obligation to deal with the question, and of course it would be open for the St. Helens Corporation to say at the end of two years that it was not convenient for them to carry out their promise. The duty will now devolve upon the Warrington Corporation to press for the insertion of a clause in the new Bill compelling St. Helens to eleal with the matter,and in this we hope they will be successful.

The committee appointed by the Board of Trade to consider whether the means of communi- cation between the passengers in railway trains and the servants of the company are efficient has condemned the outside cord system. As a matter of fact, no inquiry was needed to do this. The proposition that a frail person, probably a woman, who was held down by a ruffian in the far eorner of a carriage, would be allowed to advance to the other end, open the window, and reach out an arm to the cord, without demur by the assailant, is too absurd for contemplation. As well might one expect the burglar to oblige by blowing a whistle for his own arrest at the wish of an invalid in a bedroom. The presumption is that no adult railway traveller will raise an alarm except in extreme necessity, and that necessity requires that the means of alarm should be handy. It should be above the reach of small children, but for grown lip people the alleged temptation to tamper with it is small; and as a vexatious call would meet with punishment, practical jokers may be trusted to exercise discretion. The committee has decided in favour of electrical communication, with the means by which it can be actuated by the pas- senger either in the centre or at both ends of the compartment. They hold also that the new method should afford an indication outside the carriage that it was from this or that compart- ment the alarm was given. It now remains for the companies to put this plan into force as quickly as their convenience will permit.

Another report bearing on the comparative trade of England and Girmany has just been issued, viz. : that of Consul General Sir Charles Oppenheimer, on the trade of Frankfort and dis; trict for the year 1897. As a set off to the genera' complaint here of the way British trade is being adversely influenced by German competition the report dilates upon the popularity of British goods in Germany itself. " British goods," the report roads," are willingly bought by the classes that know how to judge, because they are looked upon as practical, solid, and agreeable, and are receiving more favour from year to year with the best classes, so that in th ) greater number of large cities special English stores are being estab- lished." This is in direct contrast to the reception accorded articles of German manufac- ture sold in this country. There is a considerable demand for such goods, we know,but more on the ground of their cheapness than intrinsic worth. A further observation which the Consul makes throws not a little light on the reason why some branches of our own trade are said to be " going." The complaint comes against the English manufac- turers that they show a lack of willingness to meet their castomers,whereas the German business man, in small or great matters meets the desires ot his business friends. With such business principles he prospers and is becoming more and more a for- midable competitor for other countries. We can readily believe that there is ground for such com- plaints, especially against our larger manufac- turers and traders. Therefore it behoves them to show a willingness to oblige in small things, even if only to counrer-balance the effect of increased Germanurbanity.

[BY A COIIII.ESPOND]NII, The topic around which centres the chief interest this weak is the all absorbing one of the appoint- ment of a clerk to the School Board. Of course, it goes without saying that a local man will get the appointment. And one has not much looking round to do, but what a hand can ba laid upan the pro- bably successful candidate. We all have friends and we all think our friend is invincibly popular. And naturally the moat popular candidate will secure the appointment.

It is whispered that the Church party will have a candidate, and the Nonconformist party will have a candidate, and the Roman Catholic party will— hold the balance. But then do those of this opinion forget that the members of the Runcorn School Board are—or ought to be—above such things as nepotism and its kind. They had no need to restrict canvassing, and I freely predict that an outsider will be elected to the post, if he is the best man.

But this is not all that is said, It is the " city fathers" that Come in for censure this ticce. Tam, had a grand opportunity of improving a street, or going a step in that direction. But no, they could not seize an opportunity, for instead of widening a a street they adopt a policy that tends to keep it narrow and allow shops to be brought out into the street, which is even now quite narrow enough. It may be argued that nothing is altered in the actual width ; but it cannot be denied that another oppor- tunity has gone by.

As every Runcornian is aware Greenvvay-road has been in truth a" green way," and to the property- owner has returned more rent to the year than many an acre of apparently better property. But, if it is to continue to be of any attraction and healthi- ness, surely it is time to protest against the inva- sion of the shop-keeper. Or, if he must absolutely be admitted into the street, should not something be done to admit him in. acceptable form? Can't he come in a manner pleasing and in harmony with the surroundings ?

It appears that the two cycle clubs that exist in Runcorn, have taken it into their heads to think that the town is not big enough to hold them both. What nonsense ! Why it is absolutely essential that there should be two cycle clubs. Now consider the case of people of two temperaments: one a fiery one—al ways longing to get on his "bike and ride ! ride ! I ride !! ! mile upon mile ; and the other timid. unventuresorae, loving to ride slowly and gently, taking in the beauties of niture, lbw else cm n those antipodes be met, but bye spacial catering.

The Runcorn Heath and Commons Provisisnal Order, has passed its third reading in the House of Commons, and soon the time will ba at hand to face the colossal task of licking that common into un- common shape. It will be a tall order. But my earnest hope is that the matter will be done sys- tematically and upon approved plans; not in the novel way of doing the whole lot at once, and doing it so badly as to have to continually patch it u;) in years to come. Now it could he doni nicely in a Period of ten or more years ; gradually bit by bit; each year's work to be continuous with the follow- ing year. Spending only a thousand pounds a year; it would be cheaply accomplished,and thus th, of maintenance for the first 10 years would he nil, virtually.

About half-past three last Friday morning a man named Richard Banner found the body of a woman in the Bridgewater CanO. Rhe was identified as Sarah Ann Downward, aged 57, a widow, of Lymm. The previous evening, it is stated, she was at th. Boat House Inn, Agden Bridge, from nine o'clock until eleven o'clock. She was seen after that hour walking along the towing path of the canal. The inquest on the body was held by Sir. J. R Wereley, coroner, at the Reatley Hotel. Evidence was given as to the woman being seen going along the canal bank at night, and it is presainxi that she fell in and an one being about she was drowned. A ver- dict of" Found drowned" was returned.

DEATH Atqrk Yunnitit. OF Mn. R. G. FA.nitINGTON. The large attendance at the Cemetery on Sunday at the funeral of the late Mr. Farrington bore testi- mony to the esteem in whicn be was held. Mr. Farrington had for many years been one of the assistant-masters at the National Schools, Church- street, and thougn he had been in ill-health for the past few mouths, his condition did not give alarm to his relativvs. A week ago serious symptoms developed, and despite the constant attention of Dr. Josaph, he passed peacefully away on Thursday June 23rd, at his resifie.nce in Marshhouse-lane. At the funeral, the coffin,. which was carried ahoulder high to the Cemetery, was preceded by a large num- ber of friends, chiefly members of of the Warring- ton North Bowling Club Amongst those present were Messrs. F. Taylor, J. D. Brimelow, A Brims- low, .T. Dewhurst (heful•master, National Schools), Willcocks, J. Allison, R Young, Gandy, J. Peacock, W. Frybr (Pailgate), whilst several of the deceased's old scholars joined in the procession at the Ceme- tery gates. Thfs bearers were Messrs. A. J. Jones, J. Whittle, J. Willett, a Taylor, W. Haigh, Woods, Podmore, Finch. The ceremony in the chapel and at the graveside was conducted in an impressive manner by the Doctor, and the coil] n bore the simple inscription " Robert G. Farrington, died Jane 23rd. 180 S, aged 33 years." .Many beautiful wreaths were seat by relatives and friends, one be- ing from the scholars of the National Schools. The members of the Warrington North (Cemetery) Bowls ing Club, of which the deceased was a member, also forwarded a floral token of their sympathy, TRE DEVON AND WESSEX ASSaCIATIONS AT WARRINGTON. A visit was paid to Warriagton on Saturday by the members of the Devon and Wessex Associations of Manchester and district. The party. which in a number of ladies, was met at the Central Statioa by Mr. W. l'i. J. Jenkins, who conducted them to Walton, a couple of large 'buses being used for conveying the visitors. The grounds of' Walton Old Hall,(Mr. F. Monks' residence) were first visited and needless to say, greatly admired. From hero it was but a step to Sir Gilbert Greenall'e residence, and where a much fuller programme of sight, seeing was provided. The party was conducted through the famous piggeries, riding-school, orchards, and greenhouses, and en-route they were shown the horses and other animals with which Sir Gilbert Greenall competed so successfully at the Royal Agricultural Show last week. After the beauties and attractions of Walton Hall had been enjoyed, the party was driven back to town and sat down to an excellent tea at the " Lion Hotel." The ' Mayor was amongst those present, and remarked that he very heartily welcomed the societies to the town, and hoped the day. was not far distant when they would see them again. They had not much to boast of in Warrington, but still he was proud of the town in a-, hich he was born 50 years ago. He wished they could have paid a visit to the Parish Church, which dated back to the 11th and l2;di century, and in which Mr. Jenkins and himself had sung for a quarter of a century. There were other ; interesting places to. be aeun, but time would not ' allow except for a aosit to the Town Hall. park and •, gardens, where he should be pleased to accompany - them. Before leaviug for Manchestir a visit was 5 paid to the Park and gardens, with which the visitors expressed thetuselvea delighted,

Mr. CooetLL asked the First Lord of the Treasury whether it was the in- tention of the Government next session to bring in a bill for the redistribution of seats, SO as to secure that on the basis of population the large towns should have the number of repre- sentatives in the House of Commons to which they were fairly entitled.— Mr. BALFOUR said he could not give any pleige as to the Parliamentary course teat would be taken by the Government, as a Reform Bill was an immediate prelude to a dissolution. The matter had engagea, and would continue to engage, the earnest attention of the Government.— Kr. H. CECIL took the oath. and his seat for East Herts. in place of the late Mr. Abel Smith. On the motion for the third reading of the Bast India Loan Bill, Mr. Herbert Roberts urged the nefiessity for classifica- tion of expenditure, so as to distaiguisli betw3en expendi- ture for Imperial purposes and that for exclusivtly Lnian purposes. Mr. Strauss asked for a pledge that none of the loan authorised by the bill should be used to change the India's monetary system. The House then went into committee on the subject of Egypt—remission of loan—and the CH kNceLt-ni, of the EXCHEQUER moved that it was not expedient tint the grant 'of £798,003 to Egypt should be repaid. After referring to the satisfactory results already achieved In the province of Dongola as the result of the expeditions a'ready undertaken, • he admitted that the next step. the advance on Khartoum. might be of a nature far more serious than anything that had yet been carried out. The Egyptian forces, however. would be supported by a larger force of British troops -than had ever before been employed there. But he lid not antici- pate that it would be necessary to retail the large nritish force for any length of time at Khartoum or in the Soudan. It was estimated that the additional cost wo drl not ecceed £75 ),000, and the Government considered thet if the loan of £793.000 made to the Egyptian Governm gat in the early part of 1897 was remitted, th 3 Egyptian Government would be able to provide all that was necessary.—Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT Said if there was to be a military occupation of Khartoum the Government's calcolati 10 Nilib not like y to be fulfilled. A ! substantial supper was provided which was much en- joyed by the guests assembled. Songs were afterwards. contributed by Messrs. W. Fryer, Sherleck, Bellian,Han- kinson. Price and Whittle. Mr. W. Whittle, humorist, caused much laugeter, hut Mr. Bellian's sentimentals certainly proved him to be the singer of the evening. A WARRINGTON MAN TRAVELLING WITHOUT • TICKET. on Friday at the Borough Police Court before the Mayor (in the chair), Dr. Gomel!, Mr. James Flepherd, and Councillor Smethurst, William Bolton, 33 York-st. , was charged wi-h travelling without a ticket on the London and North-Western Railway between Sankey Bridges and Warrington on the 27th May. Defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr.J. Fenna,solicitor,whoappeared for the London and North-Western Railway Company, said they really did not know where the defendant joined the train. They knew he went to Widnes every weak, but they had fixed upon Sankey. He was seen to get out of the train by a carriage cleaner. He had same diffi- culty in opening the door, so the carriage cleaner opened it for him. When asked for his ticket he said "I have not come by train." Bet the ticket collector said "You have,l saw you myself." He stuck to his staternent,and the ticket collector told him it was not the first time. Mr. Fenna said be thought there would be no doubt from the evidence that he had been travelling by train. He called James Blinston, ticket collector in the employ of the London and Ncrth-Western Railway Co., who said on Friday the 27th last month, he was on duty on the arrival of toe train from Liverpool at 2-16 p.m. He knew the defendant very well and saw him get out of the train and go into the urinal. Witness saw him come cut and asked him for his ticket. Defendant said be lead not come by train. Witness said "you have and it is not the first time."—Joshua Gregory, carriage cleaner said he was on duty at the low level station on the day in question. He knew the defendant very well. As the train came in he stood on the platform and saw the de- fendant attempt to turn the handle of the carriage door. He went up and opened the door for him. The defend- ant seemed to have had drink and went into the urinal. —When asked to make his statement the defendant said he had finished delivering piper in Wilson Patten-street and went on the station, and straieht into the urinal. He had never gone to Widnee on Friday. It was sooumehe inreis i al- ways Tuesday. When they vieited bun at his house about the matter, he told them sthereorrmust s see y e take.--The Mayor : I am very y thought you were a respectable man. The Bench fine you 103 and costs or 14 days. ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A WARRINGTON MAN.—I WITNESS'S EVIDENCE. On Friday, at the Borough Police Court, Richard Jefferson, of 81, Wellfield-street was charged with assaulting David Evans, Pierpoint-street.—Mr.Forshaw, who appeared for the complainant, said his client was a young man of rather simple mind. He worked at Monks Hall and Co's. Works, so did the defendant. The complainant was engagee with his work on the 15:13 met, when the defendant threw a rope round his neck, pulled it and so hurt him, that he had to stay from his work. It was not the first time the defendant had been assaulted by the werkmen.—The complainant David Evans said on the 15th lost, the defendant put a rope round his neck and about a fortnight ago he turned a tapon him and wet him through.—John Evans, father of complainant, said the defendant came to see him last Sunday night. He wanted to make it up, said he was sorry, and asked him not to take the summons out. He said if witness did not make it up it would be a bad job for the lad. He told defendant it was his duty to press the case.—Thomas Andrews was the next witness called. Mr. Forshaw : You have been Subpoened to give evidence here ?—Witness.—Yes.—By Mr. Forshaw : Witness saw the rope put round Corn- plainant'a neck. Afterwards he denied that he saw it put round his neck. Further questioned and pressed by Mr. Forshaw,and after being warned that he most speak the truth he again admitted hie first statement. Witness now got quite embarassed and began to make most con _The Miyor : Be careful now or al flictine statements. you will find yourself in a diffseorznenatfpulrsichee,r be proceeded against.—Af:er ation by Mr. Forshaw.during which witness made vary. log statements. The 51.1y0r salcl " put him Out what good is he."—Dafendant in his statement said he nee" to the boy since he had had done anything es-rc'n been working there. He Pickf'd " a rope and threw it away. When he turned round, he saw the rope had got round complainant's neck. He was cryine. He said " what is the matter David ?" Complainant replied that the rope had hurt him.—.A witness named Hatton, who also worked at Monks, Hall and Co., said he came out of the engine room. He saw defendant throw the rope behind him and it got round the COmPlain- ant's neck.—Mr. Porshaw " You ssw the rope put round

his neck ? Witness:—No I did not.—Mr. Forshaw come now, tell the truth yon have been talking this matter over P—Witness.—l have not.—Another witness namsd Knowles corroborated the previous witness. The Chair- man.—We are not quite satisfied in our minds that it has bee] done wilfully; the decision of the bench is that the case is dismissed. A WANDERING PAINTER AND His CHILDREN. On Monday at the Warrington Borough Police Court, before Mr. T. Birchall, and other magistrates, William John Nelson, a painter, and Mary Nelson, his wife, last from Knutsford, were charged with unlawfully expos- ing three of their children, aged five, three and one year old, by begging in Bridge-street in a manner likely to injure their health.—Prisoners pleaded not guilty.—ln- spector McAteer, N.S.P.C.C., stated that on Sunday, morning prisoners left Knatsford and tramped to War- rington. At 8.30 p.m., in consequence of complaints from ladies, he went to St. James-street, Latchford, where he saw prisoners and the children go into the Roan COW Public House.they came out again,andwitness followed them to Bridge-foot,where they again went into public-house with the children. The male prisoner was refused drink, and when they came out a lady gave the children some bread. The lady told the prisoners that it was a shame to tramp the children about in the rain. The male prisoner told him that he had come from Knutsford that morning, and was going to Liverpool. The prisoners went to another public-house, where the male defendant had a pint of beer and the female a glass of beer. They afterward; went to Ship-yard, where witness gave prisoners into the custody of P.C• Newey. When they were proceeding down Mersey-street, at 10-30, the male prisoner's conduct was most dis- graceful, and his language WA not fit to hear: He called upon the public to release him from the police.— P.C. Newey said that at ten o'clock on the night in ques- tion be accompanied the laspector to Ship-yard, where he found the male prisoner drunk. His wife was not so bad in drink. An hour previously they came to him to be directed to a lodging-house. Witness saw them go in- to Walker's vaults, Bridge-street. The children were wet through, and the male prisoner had 3m 51 in copper on him.—The male prisoner said be Was sorry for what had happened. Hs was a painter and paperhanger by trade, and being thrown out of work came to Warring- ton to look for some. He said 40 had 4.1 given to him in copper by a eentlernan. He met with some friends on the way to Warrington, and they bad given him di iak. —The magistrates sent prisoners to gaol for seven days, but afterwards gave them the option el a flue of 51 and costs each (El. 7) which was not pail

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday morning, before Mr. Ifirchall and other magistrates,John WiMame (24) and Tnomas Goulding (22), both of Tawi.-hill,were charged with having been drunk and disoreerly on Town-hill on Saturday night. Goulding was also charged with assaulting P.C. Dilahay while in the execution of his duty at the same time and place.—P.C. Delahay stated that at eight o'clock on Saturday night he was on duty in Horsemarket-street when he was called to Tow n- hill. He there saw the two Prisoners lighting with two other men on the ground. Be endeavoured to separate them, and a large crowd of pro-le gathered together. Goulding become very violent. Witness got hold of three of the men,but owing to the violence of Goulding he had to let one go ond the other afterwards escaped. Sergeant Evans followed him, and having captured him took him to the Police Station. Witneaa had to put the " spa "en Gouldinz, and even after that he butted him several times in the chest with his head and tried to kick him. Be also used most filthy language. A young man named Hatton :came to witness's assistance, and they had great trouble in taking prisoner to the Police Statim. Bath prisoners were drunk.—John Hatton, 18, Heaton-street, said he was in Horsemarket-street about eight o'clock, and heard a disturbance on Town-hill. He went there, and saw the two prisoners fighting. Goulding was very violent, and tried to kick the constable. Witness went to the assist- ance of the pelice.--P.S. Evans Raid he saw the crowd on Town-hill and went up. Williams had just Rot away from the constable, and witness followed and captured him, afterwards taking him to the Police Station. Goulding tried to kick the constable, and behaved very violently. A crowd of about two or three hundred had assembled.—Williams said he was not very drunk, and went quietly to the Police Station.—Goulding said he met some men and had a" sup "of drink. He had not been long home from India, and the drink took effeet on him.—The Chief Constable said Gouldine had been thirteen times before the Reich at St. Rel,ms. The con- victions rstpnded from November, 1896, to Jose of this year. Ii 1897 he was eleven times betties the magis- trates. Williams was a stranger to the p dice —Williams was committed to gaol for even flail'. and Goulding twenty-one days, both with hard labour.—Toe witness Hatton was called for by the Bench, and the Chairman informed him that he had earned the thanks of all res- pectable inhabitants in going as he did to the assistance of the police. He thought it was very creditable to him. A man in such a position had a certain amount of danger and odium to incur, and he (the Chairman) was glad to see that they had men v. ha would go to the assistance of the police when revired.—The (Thief Cone able said he had never been in a town where people so adilY gave assistance to the police.

On batarday, at the conclusion of the cricket match between Warrington and Cheadle Hulme,Dr. Reginald smith, captain of the Warrington Cricket Club, was 'presented with a handsome marble time- piece on the occasion of his forthcoming marriage. In making the presentation Councillor Pierpoint, on behalf of the subscribers, referred to Mr. Smith's abilities as a cricketer and the esteem in which he is held by a large number of members. Dr. Smith suitably replied. The clock bore a suitable inscrip- tion encraved on a braes plate.

div.head: WARRIN GTO N ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRIN GTO N ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.

A meeting of this committee was held in the Board_room at the Workhouse on Friday morning. Mr. G. Pilling presided,and there were also present: —Messrs. William Houghton, J.P.. A. Jolley, A. J. Jolley, J. Johnson, E. L. Bent, J. Billinge, with Mr. J. C. Sutton (clerk), Mr. S. Sutton (assistant clerk), Mr. Owen (valuer), and Mr. J.L. Tarlatan (assistant overseer). THE ASt'ESSMENT OF BISHOP'S WHARF. Mr. Owen presented his report as requested by the Committee with reference to the assessment of Bishop's Wharf and Shipping Company. The report ran as follows :—" At your last meeting an: appeal was made against the following assessments : Warehouse power and crane, gross £46. rateable £37 103 ; wharf, gross £97 103, rateable £B2 103 ; warehouse and additional warehouse entered in two items amount- ing to gross £64 10r. rateable £5O 103 ; total, gross £205, rateable £1.71 104. The first and last items are on the buildings and land, making a total of gross £llO 103, rarealle £B9. These ate from my valuations which have been adopted by you,and of wLich I am of opinion there should be no reduction. A receipt was produced showing the rent charged by the owners to be £lOO per annum, but I have no doubt this rent does not include the power and crane. The assessment of grew; £97 10s, rateable £B2 10; on the wharf should be reduced to gross £79 10r, rateable £67 103,inasmuch as this is the amount paid to the Corporation tor r nt and interest on outlay. A receipt was produced stating the rent to be £36 per annum but I have ascertained that in addition to this rent, "interest on outlay" to the amount of £3B 64 is paid and also a rent on the ground ot £s,making a total amount as now settled between oration. The new timber tohfe £ tenants 6asn, ts thisa n rid e i otgh hi p wharf which I was instructed to value is now in use although the upoPr 5'1144" is not yet paved. I value this at gress £26, rateable £22. Summary :—Ware- house power and crane, gross £46. rateable £37 103 ; ; additional warehouses, gross £64 10, rateable £5O 1034 wharf.gross £79 104,rateable £67 10 -; new timber wharf aross £26, rateable £22; total, gross £216, rateable £l7B 10.3.—Mr. Owen added that the lecsiptfjr £36 produced otrhpeor quest of the Company. The rtion.to divide the rent from he interest fa at the last meeting as being the annual rent wits made out :tnini:ahGtat the Assessment Committee could lie w company p ,00 tras. opkri eanoit paid on the eapithl invested in the wharf. as t wotaymtro.ritihoeu4plutzsse„ of assessment, not dividepirt,pinoslthioatn On the conded by Mr. A. Jol'ey the report was appre.ve I of LIE A:=SESSM ENT OF TUE PENKETII RECREATION G tiOUN D.

Mr. R. GARNETT appeared to appeal on behalf of the Parish council of Penketh against the assess- ment of .29 gross and £8 103. rateable on the Pen- keth Recreation Ground. He pointed out that the recreation ground was of very little service,and the Parish. Council let the herbage for lOs a year. They ; paid a rental of £1 to Mr. Hughes, the. lord of the 'manor. It was orginally £3 per annum but had been reduced. It was used by the inhabitants within a radius of three miles, and really the rate paid ought to be distributed between the three townships of Penketh, Cuerdley, and Great Sankey. The Parish Council thought it a hardship to pay on an assessment of £8 10s tor what did not bring in anything beyond 10s. a year.—The Clerk: To whom do you pay £1 7—Mr. Garnett : To the lord of the manor. Proceeding he said it was let to Mr.lOckle- shaw a great many years ago for .29.—Mr. Hough ton : Do I undemand that Cuerdley and Sankey have the right to use it 7—Mr. Garnett: That is so.—Mr. Garnett having retired whilst the committee considered their deci- sion, the clerk said it was simply a case of £9 ren- tal remaining on the books after that rental had disappeared.—Mr. A. J. Jolley thought it was a case similar to those they were considering wit reference to the Corporation.—The Clerk said be thought it was a case certainly nearer to the Lon- don case—in which a decision had been given— than the Warrington case. A rental of £1 was paid 'in the Peneeth case,and he thou!;ht the aesessment should be reduced to that amonnt.—i he Chairman: Don't you think it would be better to leave the matter over until the committee had settled the Warrington case 7—The Clerk : I would suggest that £1 is the actual rent paid. In the case of the Corporation they don't pay any rent at all.—Mr. A. J. Jolley: That rental is only a nominal rental.— The Clerk : They cannot put this ground to any other use. The best they can make out of it is lOs. a year. He thought the best thing for the committee to do was to put the asqessment at the rental paid to lilt. Hughes.—Mr. A J. Jolley pointed out that the area of the Penketh Recrea- tion Ground was much larger than that of Queens Uardens in Warrington, and yet the latter was as- sessed at £2O, and the Recreation ground at £9. The Clerk said it was a question of tenure. Public parks and gardens came under the Public Health Act but he wus inclined to think that the Penketh Recreation Ground did not come under that Act.— The committee decided to adjourn the considera- tion of the matter.—Mr. Garnett on being called into the room, in answer to inquiries by the Clerk said it was land partly belonging to the lord of the Manor and partly to the inhabitants. Mr. Owen said the enclosure Com- missioners allotted the land to the inhabitants, the Lord of the Manor reserving certain rights.— Mr. Garnett said on one portion of the land there was not a blade of grass. Two teams of footballers made use of it. There was a little herbage round the Bides, but the tenant who used it would not pay more than 10s. a year.—The Clerk informed Mr. Garnett that it was a question for the committee how far the Recreation ground came under a recent decision of the House of Lords, and the committee had decided to adjourn the consideration of the matter. THE VALUER'S REPORT.—IMPORTANT VALUATIONS. Mr. Owen (the surveyor) reported that he had made the following valuations for assessment In the township of Warrington : Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co. Ltd., Atherton's Quay. Warrington : offices and • stable, gross £124, rateable £lO5 10s., house adjoining the offices occupied by Mr. John Burthem gross £lB rate- able £l5 103., iron works, gross £24l,rateable £lB4 103. Further additions to Tube Works gross £333, rateable £249 EX—Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Limited, Bank Quay Soap Works, Warrington. The completed valuation of the Bank QUM' Soar Works up to date is gross £4,046, rateable £3,334. The previous assessment was gross £2,679 ; rateable £2,079. Mr. Londrew Rath- bore,works and yard,Lythgoes-lane,appealed against the assessment of gross £52 100., rateable £42 on account of non occupation. I have visited the works and find that beyond housing the engine and boiler there is no occu- pation to speak of. I am of opinion that an assess- ment of gross £2O, rateable £l7, would be sufficient. In the township of Cuerdley. The United Alkali Com- pany, Limited. Sullivan's Works. I wat asked to value the new:coke plant. I find on visiting the works that they had not been valued since 1876, and that alkali had been made in the Salt Cake Department anti pumps and well house erected and other alterations had taken place. I have thereforerevalued the whale of the works of Messrs. Sullivan and Co., standing in the township of Cuerdley and report them as follows :—Salt Cake Department, gross £995 104., rat( able £762 103. ; coke plant depart- ment gross £5BO, rateable £4Bl 103.; pumping station, gross £l4B 103., rateable £1.6 10.. ; sidings gross £7B rateable £5B 103. ; total gross £1,802, rateable £1,409. These figures should take the place of the existing assessment of gross £1,098, rateable £B93.—Mr. A. J. Jolley called attention to the revaluation of Sullivan's Works, and asked whether the Committee had not been losing by the under-assessment,—Mr. Owen said the committee had been lo.ing the assessment of the pump- ing house which must have been up for fifteen years. The report was adopted.

By a mere chance the Hungarian Prime Minister has made the discovery of gold on his estate at Maros- Jordea,in Transylvania. The land is said to contain an enormous gold yield, and it will be at once worked. Transylvania has been known as a gold yielding district since the most ancient times, and for some years now British and German companies have worked mines there with good returns for their investments. A trial will shortly be made at Cadiz of a new kind of :iglarnarino troat,which is said to possess perfect stability. I The boat needs neither steam nor electricity,but is driven by clockwork, and can be handled by two men. The inventor, who is a nativo of Cadiz, will offer his iraven tion to the Government. •

ANGLICAN ROMAN I 3 : CONFESSION AND
ABSOLUTION.

their eagerness in denouncing their ritualis- tic brothers as traitors and Romanisers the so-called " Evangelical " sections of the State clergy seem to for. get or ignore the fact that they do not come into the ' controversy with the cleanest of hands themselves. Broad Churchmen, Low Churchmen, and Ritualists all enter the ministry of the National Zion by the same door, and through the same form of ordinatioo,and here is the commission they all roceive alike. Humbly kneeling be- fore the Bishop that State functionary lays his hands upon them and says, " Receive the Holy Ghost for the office and work of a prie,.t in the Church of God, now committed unto thee by the imposition of our hands. Whose sins thou dost forgive, they are forgiven ; and, , whcso sins thou dost retain, they are retained." (The Ordering of Priests). A further reference to the Prayer I Book, the Churchman's auxiliary Bible, shows us that this ceremony is not intended to be a dead letter,a mere farce, but the imparting of a supernatural power. Every time the Evangelical or Itltualist priest performs Divine Service he tells the congregation that " Almighty God, the father of our Lord Jesus Christ, bath given power, and commandment to his ministers, to declare and pro• nounce to his people, being penitent, the absolution and remission of their sins." (Order for Morning Prayer). And the way in which this power is to be exercised is laid down in the clearest and most explicit manner in the same Prayer Book. Ia " The Order for the Visita- tion of the Sick." after some preliminary prayer, wa read, the sick person is to be" moved to make a special confession of his sins, it he feel his conscimco troubled with any weighty matter. After which confes- sure, the priest shall absolve him (if he humbly and heartily desire it) after this sort, " Our Lord Jesus Christ, who bath left power to his Church to absolve all sinners who truly repent and believe in him, of His great mercy forgive thee thine off, noes ; and by His authority committed to me, I absolve thee from all thy wins, In the name of the Father, and of ths Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Whether this doctrine of ' Priestly Absolution is or is not in accordance with the teaching of Holy Scripture,tve pause not to enquire. But whether true or false it it unquestionably one of the mcet impor- tant articles of the Roman Catholic faith, and the Broad and Low Churchmen who lend it their countenance and support as they do, should hesitate before throwing stones at their ritualistic brothers as traitors and Romani- sers, because they boldly teach and practice what they themselves have bean taught. If the priest has no power to forgive sins let them be honeat men and turn the doctrine root and branch out of their Church and thus save it from a good deal of scandal and unseemly controversy.—Yours truly,

The report for the year 1897 of Vice-Admiral Sir G. 8 Nares, Acting-Conservator of the Mersey, shows that. 9,122,320 tons were dredged from the Queen's Channel bar,shoals in the Queen's Channel and Crosby Channel during the tc.elve months. The send pump dr!?dgers re- moved 642,000 tons from the Prince: Landing-.ta,,e, 121,100 from the George's Landing-stai!e, and 129,700 from opposite dock entrances. The abstract of traflic through the several sea channels, recorded by the light- ships,of both inward sni outward traffie was 46,801 vessels, of wtich 40,977 used the Qieen's Channel and vessels passed the Crosby Lightsbql and Askew Spit,showing an average of 112 daily usin this channel I enter- ing or leaving the port of I;iverpool. The number using g n the Rock Channel was 5,115, and 709 pissed throe.gli the Formby Channel or cro3seid the Zebra Flats. Toe full average of daily traffic in ant out 'of the port of Liverpool was 128 vessels. There were 1,976 vsseels less tnat the total of 48.777 recorded in the previous year. The Water Bailiff's annual return shows 67 wrecks and casualties which have come under his supervision in th" course of the year. This total shows a decrease of 5 under last year. The total wreck were 13 in number. The casualties to vessels were 54 in number. Ail hands were lost from the schooner Wellington, which foundered In the Horse Channel on the 19th June, and five other lives were lost Curing the year. Under the orders of the head constable (Captain J. W. Nott Bower) the usual -care has been taken throughout the year to prevent rubbish and ashes being thrown into the river or deposi- ted on the banks.

div.head: ST. HELENS CORPORITION BILL.
div.p: ST. HELENS CORPORITION BILL.

OPPOSITION BY WARRINGTON. The St. Helens Corporation Bill, which is promoted for the construction of additional electricity works, and for the consolidation of loans, and for cetnee purposes,on Tuesday came before the Police aud Sanitary Committee of the House of Commons, over which Sir Stafford , Northcote presided, The corporation were represented by Mr. Pember, Q.C., and Mr. Farbee Leukaster, and there appeared in eppoeiti on to the seheine for tho %Vat- : rington CorPoration, Mr. Pembroke Stephens, Q.O the Lancashire County Ceuacie Mr. Worsley Taylor, Q C., and Mr. Gerald Fitzeerald ; and the Lancashire Asylutns Board, Mr. Herbert Rigg. The Liverpool Corporation also opposed the scheme,but counsel were reserved. The first opposed eart taken was the proposed extension of the borough by the inclusion of about six acree now in the county, and deecribed in the Bill, "All that portion of the township of Eccleston lying between ft Oahe!. road and the present boundary of the borough, where such amundary runs through the grounds of the Rainhill (Old) County Aeylutn.—Mr. Pilkington (Mayor of St. Helens) stated that this was a meter of no great import- ance, but the boundary waq at preeent an eyesore, and it was desired by the council that the natural boundary proposed by the Bill should be substituted. So far as rates were amaerned, the corporation would not receive any benefit, for whatever additional they got in that respect would be counterbalanced by the cost of repair- ing the road. The object was to get a defiaed boundary. —Mr. George Broom (borough engineer of St. Helens) corroborated the statement of the Mayor, and explained that at present, when the roads in that district were re- paired, it was found that a continuous repair of a par- ticular road in this area could not ba undertaken, owing to the part of it which the promoters sought to annex being under the jurisdiction of the rural district council. —Mr. Leuty said the committee could not waste their time in hearing more evidence concerning a small matter of this kind.—Mr. Lenkaster agreed that it was a most ' miserable matter fora large county council to oppose.— Mr. A. F. Mann, clerk to the rural district council, said he agreed that the propmed arrangement would be tor the convenience of the Se. Helens Corporation, as it would give them a continuous section to repair.—The committee adjourned till Wednesday morning. The; S. Helens Corp eration Bill again came before the Police and Sanitary Committee, over which Sir Stafferd Nertecote presided on Wednesday. The question of the inclusion within the boundaries of St. Helens boroueh of a piece of land belonging to the Rainhill Asylum- was again coonderel be the committee. Evidence was given by Mr. H. W. Deacon (chairman of the Hairline Asylum Committee) to the effect that the Board con- sidered it would boa dieadyaneeee to the asylum and not an advantage to St. Helens if the land wore annexed. —ln reply to Mr. M'Kenna, witness said it was a ques- tion of rates entirely, and by the proposed change the asvluM Would lose to the extent of £I4 a year. The cost of the opposition to the scheme the board were advised, would be about £BO. Mr. J. T. Wood, civil engineer, of Liverpool exereseed his entire ag,reement with the eviderr.:e of Mr. Deacon. There was no difficulty in the present, as in matte tether cases, of one authority repairing the roads of another authority. It was merely a matter of arrangement. Mr. Riga, on behalf of the Asylums Board contended that the inclusion was a matter of some importance to his cheats, because if they had to extend the infectieus hespital cr build a new asylum, then they would, if an- nexed, have to pay rates up to tla 41 , Insteau of 21. 81. as at present. N,) witnesses were called for the Lancashire County Council, who also opposed the scheme, but Mr. Gerald ' Fitzgerald, in their interests, said the inclusion WAS a , small one, but it would involve a large amount of labour and expenditure in cenaecticia with the rearraugements of county rates. The committee decided to grant the inclusion asked for. It was explained by Mr. Lankaster that moat of the clauses were Rot opposed. There was opposition, how- ever, on the part of the Warrington Corporation on sanitary grounds, but that should be taken at a later stage. The committee then proceeded to deal with the unopposed claims. On the questioa of the tramways, the Mayor of St. Helens pointed out that the corporation proposed to Supply electric traction for the tramways, and they alio proposed to arrange for the carriage of goods at reasoa- able rates on the cars. The clauses dealing with this part of the Bill were agreed to, as was also that having reference to the application of revenue.-0a the coast. derei on of the clauses dealing with street improvement:. and the compulsory purchase of land, the Mayor explained that the corporation asked that seven years more than provide! by the Act of 1.393 should be gi ien for street improvements, and four years for the compul- sory purchase of land. The improvements, he said had been postponed owing to depressed times, but it was in- tended to carry the , tri out as soon as poseible.—The ex- tensions were granted. By CiAtl92 52 power Nem sought to exempt from rating for new street Improvements any incumbent or Miuister of any church or chapel or any meeting house appro- priated to religious worship, or of any premises appro- priated for the purposes of a Sunday school, or to the Purposes of a public elementary or secondary school, or any premises appropriated partly to one and partly to other of these purpesqs. Trio committee passed the clause omitting the refer- ence to "elementary or secondary schools." ; The promoters said they would gain nothing with those words omitted, and they took tines to consider Whether they would take the clause so amended. The committee refused to grant a clause empowering the corperation to omit " E:ysiewl is " from the diseases Which have to be notified, although Dr. Harris explained that the disease was not now so common or so severe as the other diseases,and that the false notificatione caused a ereat deal of trouble and expense. The committee passed a clause permitting the Cor- poration to regulate the isiz ; of gas pipes inside a house, hut they refused to permit that regulation to extend to ' the " fittines." The committee adj -turned till Thursday.

div.head: WARGRAVE CITURCIL CHOIR.
div.p: WARGRAVE CITURCIL CHOIR.

The members of the above caoir had their annual picnic on Saturday, to Lancaster and Morecambe. The party numbering 33 including the ftev.J.Carson, rector ,and Mr. J. Burrows, churchwarden left Earlestown in reserved carriages at 720, and reached Lancaster at 930. The first business was breakfast which was panaken of at the King's Arms Hotel, Lancaster. After a ramble about Lancaster, and viewing the Castle, the party left in wagonettes at 11.30 for Morecambe. Dinner was served at the King's Arms Hotel there, and the afternoon was pleasantly spent in various ways, although the rain which fell during the whole of the afternoon greatly interfered with the enjoyment. At six o'clock tea was partaken of at the Kings Arms, and shortly after seven o'clock, Morecambe was left behind and Earlestown was reached about 9 30, Notwithstand- ing the inclement weather, the outing was thoroughly enjaye,,l, and the arrangements which were of an excellent character were carried out by Mr. E. Leyland, organist and choirmaster. VIADUCT IVORIES OFFICE STAFF TRIP. The annual outing in connection with the Viaduct Works Office staff, took place on Saturday afternoon, the destination chosen this year being Chester and llawarden. A special saloon had been provided and permission was given for the 11-52 Chester train to call at Earlestown to pick up the party which numbered 20. On arrival ;at Chester, dinner was partaken of at the Coach and Horaes,the catering of Host Barlow being all that could be desired. After dinner, laudaus were provided, and despite the heavy downpour of rain, the party set off on a circular drive to Hawarden, by way of Eeton Hall, the drive thr 'ugh the Park, in which numerous deer and rabb!ta abounded being con- siderably marred by rain. When nearing tlawarden the weather improved, and continued flue during the remainder of the day. At Hawarden a short stay W 69 made and tbe places of interest were visited. The return journey was through Hewer- den Park, passing by the Old Castle, and immedi- ately in front of the present Castle,through Brough- ton to Chester. Tea was served at the Coach and Horses, and after a ramble through the City, the homeward journey was commenced at 8-25, Earles- town being reached about 9.30, after an enjoyable out.

EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN CHURCH CHOIR: The members of this choir with several friends had their annual picnic on Saturday. The party numbered 25, and their destination being Worksop, they left Earlestown by the 7.14 train for Warring- ton. Walking across the town they joined the 9.11 train at the Central Station, a spacious saloon hav- ing been provided for their accommodation. Toe journey through the bold scenery of the Peak dis- trict was much enjoyed, and on reaching Worksop station they drove to the Royal Hotel where dianer should have been provided, but owing to the hotel being full, it was served in the Town Hall. After doing justice to the meal a coach drive of 25 miles through Welbeek, Thorsly and Sherwood Forest in the head of which stands a monstre oak known as the Major Oak " inside which 14 members of the choir installed themseives was participated in In pars of the Forest relics of Robin Hood and his merry men," espe- mally their larder, were to be seen. Toe weather, With the exception of a heavy slacaver of rain, was all that could be desired and the drive in conse- quence was rendered specially enjoyable. Tea was partaken of at the Worksop Town Hall and the party left by the 7.15 train,reaching home at 10.40 All the arrangements were carried on; by .10Sird. Deane and Davveon.

div.head: NOTES ON U. AMES Au ATHLETICS. CRICKET.
div.p: NOTES ON U. AMES Au ATHLETICS. CRICKET.

At Arpley, on Saturday, Wariington placed Cheadle Hu!me for the first, time this season. The wicket was in a saturated coadition, and not well-suited for cricket. Owing to the rain the game was not definitely concluded. Messrs. C. H. Williams and E. Rome were opposed by Dr. Smith and Thewlis. In the home captain's first over Williams was bowled, whilst Cadman had assisted to take the total to 14 when he Oen fell a victim to the fast bowler. A. E. Taylor took p!ac..e, but rain began and play was delayed twenty ini notes.

01 resumption of play the batsmen forcing the game a ciringf• was necessitated, and Bibby relieved Thewlis. Tne fop4ration, howover, was effected by Dr. Smith, Car TA ,)lor skied one into the hands of third man,Connor e.ff,cting a neat catch. H. Royle joined Rome, and the new coiner at'onee placed both bowlers to the boundary. Clarke relieved his captain, and succeeded in getting the initial batsman taken in the slips, four wickets being down for 45. With Teather as Royle's associate a long stand was made. Morgan tried in place of Clarke.wbilst Connor relieved Bibby, but runs came at a good pace, Rlyle ins narticular exhibiting tins form. B. Silcock was tried at 74 but his opening over was productive of eleven runs.

At 93 the younz bowler had tho satisfaction of getting Teatber caught at point, Morgan b 'mg applauded for the brilliant catch. A. IL Rome lielPe,d Royle to take the score to 120, the last-named being not out for a capita/ 44. Warrington had an hour's batting, and during that period Thewlis gave a fine display. E. Connor opened with the professional and from the first runs came fast and it looked likely that the runs would be knocked off. Thirts runs were chronicledin fifteen minutes, but at 40 C )nnor was caught. G. Clarke came nest and the fast rate of run get ing was maintained, the professional's placing on the off side being clever.

Clarke stayed whilst 19 runs were added,and was then bowled by a ball from leather. The Warrington cap- tain filled the vacancy and after despatching Teather for f^ur saw Thewlis do the bulk of the scoring. Near the call of time Dr. Smith was bowled by Redfern at 74,and Bibby arrived to sea the addition of four runs without having a ball and at 642 the math was left drawn. Thewlis gave a sound display, never making a bad stroke, and he was accorded a hearty reception on re- turning to the pavilion.

The weather at Cheadle on Saturday on the orcanion of the visit of the Warrington second eleven was not Promising for their meeting for the first time this season. M home winning the toss elected to bat and ran P Eli. up a score of 94. The bowling of the visitors was gool Corsar taking 3 for 9 runs and R Pierpoint 3 for 17. Adamsvn and Crompton commenced the Warrington innings against the bowling of Horsley and Jaffreys,and with the former's third bell (b-fore anything had been scored) got rid of Adamson by Smith taking a fine catch at point. •

Unsworth next j lined Cromoron and runs came at a good rate until the score was 32 and Crompton was run out by Unsworth in trying to get a short run. R. Pier- point cams next but did not stay long being bowled of his pads off a ball from Jeffreys. Dackworth followed and batting well was out to a catch at point. Unsworth after battite• nearly an hour was caught at point for a well played 25.

Kirhoonnell and Whittaker raised the score to 94 before Kirkconnell was bowled by floosley for 15. Some of the leg hits of the last named batsman were very fine in deed. Wanting enly 1 run to win, Thompson was next in, and after playing for a considerable time made the winning hit ; Warrington thus gaining their first victory this season by 16 runs.

The watch between Grappenhall and Stockton Heath on the ground of the latter resulted in an easy win far the visitors. The hemesters batted first. The whole of the team were got out for low scores. Warburton bowled in fine style, taking sir wicket e for 12 runs. England batted neatly for the homesters. England and Howard faced the visitors, and later were relieved by Shaw and Gleave. Grappenhall played a good game. Evans and Carter batted in fine form.

At Arpley on Saturday the Workingmen's Mission played Irlam. The visitors batted first. A. Bell was in first class form, and by splendid batting compiled a score of 56 not out. J. Brooks' wicket was taken for 14 runs, and Etchells succumbed to, a catch at 17, both having hatted well. Strover was bowled by Pilling after a neat 10. Itlam closed their innings for 100 runs for the lops of three wickets. Williams for the Mission made a short stand for 12. The bowling of the visitors proved almost as good as their batting and seven wickets had fallen for 30 runs when the game was left a draw.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

Oa Saturday at the Oroch;morough C.C. Sports W. Collin, of Warrington, had matters all his own way in the tsso bicycle events. With 55 yards start in the half mile he went to the front two laps from hometand after pieinz his men into the s:raight wan easily, sitting up, by two lengths, la the mile race he repeated the per- formance, and won by three leneths in 2min. 58sees. His silo wance was 125 yards. In the mile novice handi- cap at New Brighton Tower Grounds on Saturday S. Grant of Warrington was beaten by two lengths.

It is not mere luck that makes a machine withstand a severe shock and then subsequently break down under scarcely any extra strain. It is a property of steel that when it is exposed to a considerable strain which is not quite strong enough to fracture it, it is for a time more brittle than usual. For example, a steel wire capable of standing a strain of 95 tons to the square inch if tested to 80 tons will stand it satisfactorily, but if very soon after it be loaded only to 60 tons it will snap asunder. The simo thing may happen in cycle parts,and the mar- gin of safety in them is remarkably small. They may go near to breaking, but survive the shock, and actually collapse later under less violent conditions. They have often been observed to do so, and riders have attributed to luck the fact that their accident did not occur when they were going fast or crashing down a rough bill.
In a twenty miles paced bicycle raco at Mahatan Beach, New York, on Saturday, Linton beat Titus by five-sixths of a mile in 35 min. 594-5 sec. This is the world's record.

The on record in which cyclists have been struck by lightning are extremely few in number, but an alto- gether excPptional one occurred last week to a doctor when riding through a thunderstorm near Cork. His machine was wrecked, but he was untouched by the lightning and only slightly damaged by the fall.

div.head: Wkl'Elt POLO.
div.p: Wkl'Elt POLO.

A very keen nontest.tOOl-r—Ce at the Warrington Baths on Tuesday in the polo competition between War- rington and Everton. The game concluded with one goal to the credit ot the visitors. This was a shot by Reyes, one of their backs. To the surprise of all the goal scorer raised his flag and the referee gave it in as a goal. The spectators vented their disapproval by hooting him and threats of "Chuck him in,"vrhich were not likely to have any effect on a man with any firmness of character. Such unsportsmanlike conduct should be strongly dis- continued. At the same time, there was to a certain extent reason far It. Both teams were commencing play after the shot, not thinking I,er a moment the scorer would give it in as a goal. The members of the Everton team to a man expressed themselves very decidedly about it. It was no goal they said. Reyes who made the shot when he saw the scorer raise his flag, raised his hands to the referee to explain it was no goal, but the referee had given his decision. The locals were very undecided whether to resume play or not, but they shewed their good sense in doing so, as it would serve no good purpose to do otherwise.

div.head: EMBEZZLEMENT FROM COLLIERY PROPRIETORS AT HAYDOCK.
div.p: EMBEZZLEMENT FROM COLLIERY PROPRIETORS AT HAYDOCK.
THE RESULT OF GAMBLING.

At the Newton Petty Sessions on Thur33ay before Captain Withington (in the chair), Colonel Wood, and I Mr. C. B. F. Borron, Walter Strange. 15 years of ace, living at Haydock, was charged with feloniously em- bfzzling certain sums of money araounting altogether to £4 as. Bd. on the 16th May and other dates,teloneing to Messrs. Richard Evans and Company, of Haydock. Mr. Swift, prosecuted on behalf of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. and Mr. Stuart was for the defendant. Mr. Swift said the defendant had been in the employ of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., for 14 months 411 one of their clerks in the wages office. 'rho defendent had pleaded guilty to the charge, and as be had borne a pre- vious good eharact er,they did not wiah to preis the case. It was only just, ho said,that thperfosscetesuotrts loheecmapsesyhieod a should be put before the court. The to great number of colliers, about four or five thousand and of course, they employed a great narmier of clerks to make up the wages of the men. The manager put down the nuother of dare work done by ealh man iii a book. The book came into the hands of defendant and other clerks at the head office on the 13diJune. The managers book in respect to the Queen's Pit was seat to the office, and went into the defendant's hands en the morning of the 16tla,and in the course of ordinary events should have been lent back to the manager's office. On this morning another youth named Arnold in the pay office with the defendant, observed defendant, making alterations of the amounts which would be payable to a particular collier. Be asked him what he was altering it for. The defendant muttered some unintelligable reply. The youth looked at the book later and found some other alterations. Be communicated with the pay clerk who examined the hock and found things wrung. Alteration had been made in figures 41 to si (Jaye whion made a difference of £1 33 4d.That was that the firm had to pay that amount to some nne more than they ought to pry. On the 9th and 16 h May he extracted from the firm two stuns of £1 12s. Bd. each. The defendant admitted he had made the alterations when spoken to and that he bad succeeded in stealing £1 3s. 41. and the other amounts mentioned. He had made preparations for the 11.6 ch Jane for stealing other sums but he was discovered before the pay took place, and he did not succeed in getting the sums of £1 O. 5. and £l. 83. that he had arranged to take. The frauds involved two alterations. By the figures being altered in the books to Bor 9 the collier was to draw wages for those many hours. The ticket was made out in favour of the collier for the number of hours stated. But the fraud weteld net be completed because the collier would not receive the ticket for the large amount unless some further alterations were made, and the defendant could only do it when the men were being paid. His course was to substitute the altered tickets for the tickets of which had been previously made out by another clerk. The defendant had written a statement which Mr. Swift read to the beach. The terms of the statement were as follows I calefees I have been guilty of making the followine, alterations : Os May 2ad I altered 41 dap to read 9t which meant five days in excess of the number worked by the collier. This meant an increase in wages of £1 33. 41. May 9:I), I altered William Etas figures from one day to read nine. This represented £ll2i. 81. The following day I altered a figure from one to read nine which again'rnade a difference of £112i.81. On the 18th June, I made another alteration. The method pur- sued was to alter the wages book when it Caine to the office, to a larger number of days and correct it after- wards to its previous figure on Thursday before the book went back so that the manager would have no suspicicn. I have also made an alteration of Ed w trd 42utton's hours which made them read nine days instead of four."—Nlr. Swift said the firm were exceedingly sorry that the youth who had borne a previous good name should have brought himself to that poeitiou. The defendant at this point said he had lost all the money by card playing and none was left. Mr. Swift continuing said the firm up to this were of opinion that they had effectually protected themselves. Mr. Stuart admitted that the fraud was a very ingeni- ous one. But it had come across his mind that a youth who bad only been in the place twelve months and was only 15 years of age could not have done it on his own initiation. He pointed out that no matter what his friend had said there must be something wrong to allow a boy in the presence of others to abstract money from a box and also to substitute tickets for others. Be asked the Bench to take into consideration all the circumstances and deal with him as leniently as they possibly could,and in conclusion ho appealed to the mag- istrate. to deal with his client under the First Offender's Act. He was certain the firm would not object. The Chairman said the bench did not like to ruin the young man's career and so they had decided to bind defendant over to come up for judgment when called Upon,

div.head: COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS.
CAGE PRECIPITATED DOWN A PIT. FIFTEEN MEN INJURED.

One of the most serious colliery accidents that has happened in S:. Helens district for a considerable time occurred on Monday night at the Bold Colliery, belong- ing to the Collin's Green Colliery Company, S. Helens, It appears that about nine o'clock fifteen men entered a cage to descend the No. 3 shaft of the new pit. They started for the bottom in the usual way, but the engine suddenly raced off at full speed, with the result that the men were literally thrown down the pit. The conse- quence of the impact at the bottom of the shaft upon the fifteen moo who were crowded together in a cage was most serious. They were all terribly shaken, and many of them had bones broken. As soon as possible arrangements were made fer bringing the men up the other two shafts of the colliery. Tney were received at the top by Mr. Andrew Jackson, manager. Mr. William Southern, secretary of the Company, and other officials. Dr. Jackson, of St. Helens, was at once sent fnr, and by his direction nine of the men were sent to the Providence Hospital, St. Helene. With the exception of two, they were all suffering from broken legs and ankles, as well as other injuries. Of the remaining two, one had his jaw broken and the other is suffering from severe shock. The injuries of those admitted to the hospital are as follows: —Grimes, compound fracture of ankle and right leg broken: M'Cabe, broken ankle and injury to back ; Birchen, broken ankle; Davies, jaw broken; Whittle, ankle broken; Bullen, leg broken; Garner, thigh broken; Moore, ankle broken; and Melling, shock. The engine-winder's explanation is that the engine ran away. The empty cage dashed into the head-gear on the surface,and the wire-winding rope became detachedt The strain upon it was so great that on its liberation to lashed about the engine-house, completely wrecking the roof, while engine-winder Joseph Haughton had a very narrow escape. The colliery was idle on Tuesday, the accident necessitating the stoppage of 350 men. The men are all progressing favourably.

PRIMITIVE METHODISM AT PRESTON BROOK. The anniversary sermons in support of the Sun- day schools were preached in the Primitive Method- ist Chapel on Sunday, when large congregations at- tended. The Rev. C. Finch,of Warrington, formerly of this circuit, preached on each occasion. Special hymns, &c.,were rendered by the choir and friends, Miss Cowap presiding at the organ. Although the weather was very unfavourable, especially dur- ing the evening , the collections during the day amounted to nearly .£ll, a sum considered very satisfactory. —On Monday following the Sunday school scholars were given their annual summer treat in the shape of tea and sports. &c. About 40 assembled at the cbapel, and at 4-30 were given a good tea in the schoolroorn,after which all repaired to a field. placed at their disposal by Mr. Henry Whitlow. Here games of all kinds suitable for children were indulged in until after dusk, when a pleasant evening was brought to a close. The fol- lowing teachers were present aiding in the child- ren's enjoyment:—Misses E. and A. Spruce, Miss E. Cowap, Miss Basnett, and Messrs. Wilkinson, J. Roughsedge, and H. Lightfoot, HENRY ROWE'S GALLANTRY. —A MEDAL FROM THE PRINCE OF WILES. The following is a copy of the letter of Monday's date received by Mr. Talbot, from the secretary of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem :—Sir.—With reference to my letter of the 14th December last, I have the honour to inform you that his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales. Grand Prior of the Order, has fixed Friday, the Bth of July, at Marl- borough House, for the presentation of the awards which nave been conferred during the past twelve months upon those 'who have rescued or endea- voured to save life on land at imminent personal risk. I shall therefore be glad if you will kindly arrange for Henry Rowe to attend here al the Chancery, St. John's•gate' Clerkenwell, at eleven o'clock, on the morning of the Bth July, in order that he may accompany me with the other recipi- ents to Marlborough House, to receive the bronze medal which has been awarded to hirn.—l am, yours faithfully. HERBERT C. PERROTT,

ALLEGED DEATH OF COMMODORE SCLILEY. WASHtNGTON, THURSDAY. The following telegram from Kingston (Jamaica) i& published here :—The Spanish Consul has received & cablegram from Santiago de Cuba reporting that the United States cruiser Brooklyn has been struck by & Spanish shell and sunk,and that Commodore Schley and twenty-four men have been killed. The Spaniards here are jubilant over the news. It is also reported that an extensive mine has been laid, which will blow up hair the American army when it eaters Santiago. The Cow sul attaches credence to both reports.
THE NEWS DISCREDITED AT WASHINGTON.
WASHINGTON, THLTRSDAY.

The report from Kingston (Jamaica) that the United States cruiser Brooklyn has been blown up is discreaited in official circles. It is pointed out that Admiral Samp- son would have reported the disaster if it had been a fact.

Haves, P" the third Is. by Mr. R. Sherlock. PROVERBS FOR CYCLISTS. As a pair of wheels that run truly With a pleasant murmuring, so is the talk of man and wife in a bowie which is well ruled. As the noise of a cheap crock which rattleth, so hl dissension in the house of a niggard and a sloven. The inches of our gear are three score and ten, and though there be some so strong that they ride four score, yet is their epeed but labour and sorrow at th° day's end when they fetch their wind short upon all hill. Blessedi s the damsel whose cruse of nil faileth Oct, and who looketh to her own tires ; and behold, he that taketh her to wife shall prosper. Three things are plagues to a wheelman, yea, and a fourth is abominable, a boy which leadeth an unroll horse, and a swine which atrayeth in the road, and a rash woman among traffic which regardeth not tbe right hand or the left; but the most grievous is a Countl Council which scattereth heaps of stones in the highwa9 and saith, " It is well mended." My son, beware of inventors which promise marvel: bus things with their month, lest when thou putteaa thy trust in their many inventions thou be overthroVhl in stony places. Take heed unto thy riding in strange boroughs, and fall not into transgression of their by-laws, lest thou he worsted in striving with them that swear valiantly be- fore the judgment-seat. Of two manner of people thou shalt have a care, and flee from the third as an host of the heathen; a deaf mall which walketh in the darkness, and children which ruh violently out of school at noontide, and a constable with girded loins who lurketh after sunsetting.—" Cornbill Magazine." -•• WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTif OF WARRINGTON.
